events.title: A Ukrainian air-defense sergeant says missiles aren't his most challenging shortage. It's the gear that finds enemy targets.
events.summary: MANPADS can stop Russian drones, missiles, aircraft, and helicopters. AP Photo/Andriy Andriyenko, File A Ukrainian sergeant said supporting gear is harder to get for his air defense unit than missiles. It uses MANPADS that down Russian jets and aircraft, but needs batteries and ways to find targets. Equipment like drone detectors and electronic warfare systems is "hard to get," he said. The hardest shortage facing one Ukrainian shoulder-fired air-defense unit isn't necessarily missiles, its battery sergeant told Business Insider. It's some of the equipment that helps crews find targets and keep their systems running. The soldier, who uses the call sign Yankee, serves in a front-line unit equipped with man-portable air-defense systems , or MANPADS, which fire shoulder-launched missiles able to engage low-flying aircraft, as well as cruise missiles and drones. Weapons like these, which include the US Stinger, Polish Piorun, and Soviet-designed Igla, have  been a key part  of Ukraine's short-range air defense in front-line areas, protecting troops and operations from attacks. Yankee said that for him, at least, one of the hardest things "is finding resources. Secondary resources, not the weaponry, but electronic warfare stuff." He said some of the devices that help his team detect threats and keep its equipment working are "hard to get." What is hardest to find is "mostly electronics." "I'm talking more about devices that locate the drones and warn you," Yankee said. "I'm talking about stuff like EcoFlows, batteries, big batteries, because we have a shortage of them, just in general, just a mass shortage." Ukraine's soldiers are using drone detectors to pick up on incoming Russian drones. Zoriana Stelmakh/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Ukrainian soldiers are increasingly using drone detectors, including small handheld or vehicle-mounted models, to warn of certain incoming enemy drones by detecting their radio frequencies . EcoFlows are portable power stations that can power or recharge essential gear such as radios and communications equipment, Starlink terminals, laptops and tablets, drone equipment, electronic warfare systems, and sensors. These, and batteries in general, are especially important because soldiers are often far from power outlets, and Russian attacks often shut down energy infrastructure. Running a portable generator would be much louder and might reveal their positions. Electronic warfare systems are also vital for Ukraine as it tries to disrupt Russia's communications and jam its drones. Despite their importance, this equipment isn't always easy for units to obtain in sufficient quantities. Some of the gear is much newer and less readily available than supplies like ammunition. And while demand is high, some equipment still isn't being produced in large quantities. In some cases, there are also distribution bottlenecks that affect availability. Unlike many Western militaries, Ukraine's military doesn't have a highly centralized system for weapons procurement. Units often buy or receive gear themselves, including through crowdfunding. There are advantages to this setup for  rapid innovation  because units engage manufacturers directly, but the system can also result in uneven distribution, leaving some units facing shortages. Ukrainian foundations, units, and other groups that are involved in sourcing and crowdfunding equipment for troops often ask for gear like batteries and detectors, with some describing them as items that air defenders regularly need. Ukrainian forces want electronic warfare systems to jam Russia's communications and drones. credit should read Pavlo Bahmut/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images MANPADS and the units that operate them are important for Ukraine. Units, service members, and officials have reported missiles taking down Russian drones, helicopters, and aircraft, and Western analysts have credited MANPADS with making penetrating low-altitude Russian fixed-wing and helicopter sorties too costly for Russia to continue. A report last year from the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a US think tank, said that Ukraine's integration of MANPADS operators into its air defense teams forced Russian pilots to choose between flying high and being targeted by ground-based air defenses or flying low and facing MANPAD missiles. These short-range defenses relieved the pressure on Ukraine's ground-based systems, allowing them to "survive and eventually recover." Yankee's unit provides air defense for infantry who need to get to the zero line, the far edge of the front line, and, as a result, "we participate in battle," he said. He said that conditions there can be so dangerous that moving just 300 meters can take 7 days of waiting for safe conditions and protection. Moving even that short distance, he said, "can be like a question of life and death." Yankee spoke with Business Insider at Operation Legio, a Norway-led multinational program that trains and equips Ukrainian forces, including at a purpose-built camp in Poland. He said he was learning NATO standards and tactics, combining Western practices with his existing battle-won skills before returning to Ukraine. Yankee said he uses the Stinger and Igla systems. Ukrainian soldiers have, at times since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, reported shortages of MANPADS missiles, saying those shortages allowed Russian forces to be bolder because they knew the Ukrainians couldn't try to stop as many of their attacks. But Ukraine's military has not suffered critical shortages of them the way it has with larger, surface-to-air missiles, and allies have announced new deliveries throughout the war. Not everything is consistent across the force though. Ukraine's military disseminates weapons and ammunition according to operational need, so one unit could be well supplied for critical missions while another comes up short. events.title: I moved abroad when flights home were cheap. Now caring for my aging dad is much harder and more expensive.
events.summary: The author (left) said living far away from her dad has made it difficult to help him as he ages. Courtesy of Victoria Peel Yates. I moved to Italy to be near my partner's aging parents. Now it's my dad who needs help. Flights have been getting more and more expensive, so it's hard for me to get home to help him. I feel torn between the life I built in Italy and a parent who needs me in the UK. When I threw a party in Italy to celebrate my 40th birthday, it felt like the start of a new chapter. Watching my dad attempt conversation with my partner's family across the language barrier , and my nephew playing with his nephew, I felt a joy I hadn't known since before my mom died. A year earlier, we'd decided to move to Italy to be near my partner's parents , who are older than my dad. After years in Spain, where we met, it felt like the responsible choice. Learning from my mother's death (I hadn't seen her for two years when she died because of the pandemic), I encouraged him to spend time with them while he still could. I didn't think my dad would be the one who needed help first. My dad was supposed to be the healthy one Despite having diabetes, my dad's health had held up well since my mom died, and he loves to joke that he's indestructible. I know that's not really true, but he is surprisingly resilient. There was just one small cause for concern: a persistent shortness of breath that had started about two years earlier. It wasn't very noticeable at first, but it's gotten progressively worse. He kept going to his doctor, who kept telling him everything was fine. Shortly before my birthday, the doctor had even told him the problem could be psychosomatic. My dad has always been a bit dramatic about his health, so I accepted this explanation. After lunch in a picturesque Italian village, we made him climb a steep hill, thinking the fresh air would do him good, despite the fact he'd needed airport assistance on the way over. My dad was hospitalized, and I couldn't be with him After he flew back home, he was hospitalized with a lung infection . A few days later, he was able to go home — in a taxi, because there was no one to pick him up. He was still so weak that when he fell in the garden that week, it took him ten minutes to get up. No neighbors came to help. I felt desperately sad for him in his house alone, unwell, and unable to take care of himself, but my partner and I were in the middle of moving our entire lives — including our cat — from Spain to Italy, and I couldn't get on a plane. My brother flew from Ireland to spend a few days with our dad. Once the move was over, so did I. By then, the hospital had ordered further tests, and he'd finally been referred to a specialist. The specialist suspects a serious progressive lung condition — one with no cure, although treatment can alleviate symptoms and slow its progression. We're still waiting for the full diagnosis and treatment plan. I built my life around a world that no longer exists The world has changed since I first moved to Europe over a decade ago. Britain left the EU , which means my partner can't just follow me to England — he's an EU citizen, we're not married, and I don't meet the income requirements to sponsor him. And the cost of travel has risen significantly: a round trip to where my dad lives easily costs £500 (around $678 USD) now. When I moved abroad, my parents were 60, easyJet flights cost as little as £20 (around $27 USD), and the EU's freedom of movement made the distance feel almost theoretical. That world doesn't exist anymore. Now my dad is 73, alone, and facing a serious diagnosis. My brother and I have encouraged him to get a panic button and even move to Ireland. In the meantime, I'm in a half-furnished flat in a country that doesn't feel like home, torn between trying to build a new life and a parent who needs me in England. events.title: Remaking the biscuit: from Doritos to digestives, why the UK’s snacks are being ‘reformulated’
events.summary: Healthy eating rules are forcing brands to recook their recipes. Are consumers noticing the difference? B ite into a Ritz cracker today and you’re eating 80% less saturated fat than you would have been just a few years ago. The biscuit looks and snaps the same, and tastes close enough that most buyers have no idea they’re eating a new recipe. One of the biggest changes was swapping palm oil for sunflower oil, but there was much more to it than that. The reformulation took years to perfect in a laboratory, where scientists tested everything from density to how the cracker responds to heat, moisture and packaging. It’s a story playing out across an entire industry. From Doritos to digestives, Britain’s best-loved snacks have been re-engineered, gram by gram, to meet stricter government rules on foods high in fat, sugar and salt. BelVita’s soft bakes range, including its bestselling choc chip and choc hazelnut flavours, has been reformulated to fall outside the “less healthy” category, with sodium cut by 56%. Since January 2026, paid-for advertising of high-fat, salt and sugar (HFSS) products was banned online entirely. Now the industry faces a fresh problem: the government is reviewing the formula that decides which foods count as “less healthy” in the first place. Food companies warn the changes could undo years of work overnight – the Food and Drink Federation estimates 80% of reformulated products could fail under the new model, particularly on sugar. Earlier this month at the Reading Scientific Services Ltd (RSSL) – the lab where, for many of Britain’s snack foods, recipes go to get rebuilt – that tension is being discussed. Mondelēz International, the global food and beverage giant behind Oreo and Ritz, has invested £40m since 2020 in reformulation work. The UK is now the company’s largest research and development hub anywhere in the world, with more than 750 scientists and engineers working across nutrition and product innovation at Bournville consumer research centre and RSSL. The government is proposing a tougher Nutrient Profiling Model (NPM), including stricter thresholds for free sugars and greater weighting for fibre. The changes could mean some products that manufacturers have already changed to reduce sugar are classified as “less healthy”, potentially bringing them within advertising and promotion restrictions. Jacinta George, managing director at RSSL, says the current nutrient profiling model, drawn up in 2018, counts “free sugars” against a product’s score but there’s no settled definition of what that term actually means. “The inclusion of free sugars in the 2018 NPM model is incredibly challenging for manufacturers, as there is no universally agreed definition of what a free sugar is,” George says. “There is also no standardised laboratory method for distinguishing between intrinsic and free sugars.” Swapping out sugar isn’t as simple as removing it, either. “Sugar does more than sweeten – it provides texture, bulk and preservation,” George says. “Sweeteners provide sweetness but not these other qualities, meaning additional bulking agents or functional ingredients may be needed. This can increase processing, and potentially conflict with consumer demand for simpler formulations.” The science of taking a cracker apart Reformulation at RSSL runs through several disciplines in sequence. Kerry Tanner, a group leader on the product development team, works on ingredients first – often starting with sauces and cooking bases, where salt reduction is a frequent target. “If we’re trying to reduce the score, we might be working on a sauce, and we’re trying to reduce the salt,” she says. “We used a natural alternative to salt that has a lower sodium content.” Because sauces already carry complex layers of flavour, she adds, a modest cut often goes unnoticed by the consumer. RSSL also draws on a network of culinary chefs, who work alongside the product developers on new formulations. Next comes texture – the domain of specialist Emma Nelson, whose job is making sure a reformulated product still behaves the way people expect. Complaints, she notes, can come down to something as small as how quickly a biscuit softens in tea. Every reformulated product goes through stability testing, checking shelf life and structural performance under different conditions once ingredients change. The team frequently turns to 3D printing to build physical models of a product’s internal structure, allowing them to take it apart and reassemble it to study how it holds together. Downstairs, an industrial CT scanner takes that analysis further. As colleague George Middleton explains, the machine fires X-rays through a sample; denser materials absorb more energy, and thousands of rotating scans are stitched together into a full 3D dataset of the product’s internal structure. BelVita went through the same process during its own reformulation.

events.title: I tracked how much time I spent managing my family's finances. What I found shocked me.
events.summary: The author spends about 16 hours each month managing her family's finances. Courtesy of Katherine Frankowski To understand what was consuming my time, I tracked everything I did in my off hours for one month. I was shocked to learn how much time I spent managing my family's finances. Coming to terms with the workload helps me take pride in it — and recognize its value to my family. To better understand which tasks were consuming my non-working hours, I tracked everything I did in my off hours for one month. I was shocked to learn how much time I spent managing my family's finances. Coming to terms with the size of the workload helps me take pride in it—and recognize its value to my family. <body> A few months ago, I was feeling too busy, and I wanted to know why. I knew how many hours I was giving to work each day, but where exactly were my non-working hours going? I decided to track everything I did in my weekday off hours for one month. My most surprising finding? How much time I spent managing my family's finances. It's an important but hidden role Tracking my weekday off hours confirmed some things I already knew. For example, I knew I was spending a lot of time shuttling my three school-age kids around. I also knew that housekeeping, meal planning , and grocery shopping were taking up big chunks of time, too. But I didn't realize how much time I was spending on my family's financial health. It's not that I didn't realize I was the one paying the mortgage or monitoring the checking account. It's that I somehow lacked a conscious understanding of how much time these tasks collectively took — until I tallied up the hours. I tracked my activities during my weekday off hours in 15-minute increments. At the end of the month, which was not unusual in any way, I tallied 16 hours of financial work. This means I was spending about 10% of my off-hours managing my family's finances. I checked the math three times before I could believe it. These tasks add up How could I be so unaware of how much time I was spending on my family's financial health ? One reason is that the work consists of countless small tasks: removing a duplicate credit card charge, tracking down the beneficiary form for an old 401(k), comparing insurance premiums. These tasks undoubtedly add up, but they are also hard to tally mentally. Another reason I didn't realize how much time I was giving to my family's financial health is that I usually do the work alone. I break down our monthly spending alone. I check the balances on our investment accounts alone. No one else ever really sees the financial work I do for my family, so perhaps it was easy for me to not really see it either. Understanding the amount of work was bittersweet Getting my head around how much time I devote to managing my family's finances was bittersweet. What if I'd spent those 16 hours exercising that month? Or hanging out with friends? Time is precious, and I was giving more of it than I realized to our finances. But at the same time, discovering the true size of the job gave it a kind of gravity, or importance, that helps me take pride in the work. Yes, managing our finances takes real time—but that's because it matters. Even the busy work matters. When I look at the list of things I did that month to improve my family's financial health, I see tracking, evaluating, forecasting — the work of a CFO. So that's what I call myself now: my family's CFO. I hope readers who are doing this often-invisible but meaningful work for their own families will start running with this title, too. events.title: Macy's CEO Tony Spring shared these 4 career tips from his 4 decades in retail
events.summary: Macy's CEO Tony Spring. Business Wire/AP Macy's CEO Tony Spring shared a raft of career advice during a recent podcast interview. The retail-industry veteran championed listening, connecting, and making first impressions count. Spring learned one lesson at age 16 after he was tasked with cleaning a Burger King parking lot. Shut up and listen, connect with your coworkers, and make a stellar first impression. Macy's CEO Tony Spring shared those three pieces of career advice, drawn from around four decades of working in department stores, during the latest episode of the "How Leaders Lead with David Novak" podcast. Before taking the top job at Macy's in February 2024, Spring spent around 35 years at Bloomingdale's, climbing the corporate ladder from a store trainee in 1987 to CEO between 2014 and 2023. Here are four key lessons he learned along the way: Listen and learn Don't hit the ground running, Spring said on the podcast. "I'll cut your legs off," he joked. " Hit the ground listening ." "Honeymoons come once," Spring continued. "You want to learn. This is your time. No one's expecting anything. You actually have the clearest view when you come into the company." New employees don't know enough about their employer to have the right answers, but they bring a fresh perspective as they "see things that we've stopped seeing," he added. Spring has made listening a priority for himself. "I read every customer note I receive," he said during an earnings call last fall. Show your heart Spring said that early in his career, he planned to keep his head down, get things done, and outwork everyone around him. But he recalled one of his bosses telling him that people could see his shirt, his jacket, and his glasses, but "only you can show them your heart." Those words are a reminder, Spring said, that "smiling, laughing, sharing some stories, being interested about what their lives are all about, is the smallest and simplest thing I can do, and can make the biggest difference in how people feel at work." Clean the parking lot Spring recalled that when he turned up for his first day of work at Burger King at age 16, he was dispatched to clean the parking lot . The future Fortune 500 CEO only found out why after he was done. His team explained to him that the parking lot was "the customer's first impression, and everyone who works at this restaurant has to understand how important that first impression is ." Spring said the second thing he learned was that "even though it looked like a lot of fun to work the fryer, it gets very hot." "Get out of the fry station as quickly as possible, learn how to work the drive-thru," he quipped. Stay humble Spring said that " humility is not the absence of confidence or competence." He said that as a CEO, he's found it valuable to let his workers call him by his first name and see him wearing jeans. He makes a point of talking to them about their families, and acknowledging when "something special or something terrible happens in their lives." Spring said that he sees Macy's as a "big family" whose members "care about each other." "And if we do that, then we're going to care even more about the consumer," he said. events.title: German insurer Allianz weighs $8.6 billion takeover of AA roadside rescue giant: Report
events.summary: Allianz is one of a small number of parties which have been holding talks with advisers to the AA about a deal. German insurer Allianz is considering a £5 billion takeover of AA, the British roadside rescue company. AA was founded in 1905 and went public on the London Stock Exchange in 2014 at £2.50 per share. Private equity firm EQT is another bidder, and AA’s current owners, which delisted it in 2021, are also considering a public listing as an alternative to a sale. BENGALURU – Germany-based financial services company Allianz is considering a £5 billion (S$8.6 billion) takeover swoop for AA, the breakdown recovery group, Sky News reported on Aug 29. AA, founded by a group of motoring enthusiasts in 1905 and known in Britain for its yellow recovery vehicles, was taken public on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) by its previous private equity owners in 2014 at £2.50 a share. Allianz is one of a small number of parties which have been holding talks with advisers to the AA about a deal, Sky News said, adding that private equity firm EQT was another bidder. The AA’s current private equity owners which took over the company in 2021 have been pursuing a so-called dual-track process for most of 2026, with the alternative to a sale being once more a public listing on the LSE, Sky News said. Both companies declined to comment. The Financial Times reported in 2025 that the British roadside recovery company was eyeing a £5 billion sale and was seeking buyers. REUTERS

events.title: Bryan Johnson tackled human longevity. Now he wants dogs to live forever.
events.summary: Bryan Johnson with his new dog, Katara, at a longevity event in San Francisco this week. Ben Bergman/Business Insider Johnson recently adopted a professionally trained Belgian Malinois to protect him from attackers. The new dog piqued his interest in extending dogs' lives. He plans to put his dog through the rigorous data collection and interventions he does for himself. Tech entrepreneur Bryan Johnson has become famous for his mission to help humans live forever, with his catchphrase "Don't die." Now he wants to do the same thing for dogs. Johnson's interest in canine longevity was piqued when he recently adopted a professionally trained Belgian Malinois named Katara to protect him from attackers. This week, at a longevity event in San Francisco, Katara was a constant presence at Johnson's side as he cheered on tech workers trying to complete as many push-ups as possible, one metric used to measure their biological age. Later, Katara, who will turn two in October, lay patiently at Johnson's feet as he was interviewed by venture capitalist Sarah Guo. "I get quite a few death threats, and so she is my guard dog," Johnson explained to Guo. "We go everywhere together, and we have bonded for the past month." I got a dog. Dog owners have about a 24% lower risk of dying early. What should I do now? pic.twitter.com/eOqo1zZowZ — Bryan Johnson (@bryan_johnson) August 20, 2026 Johnson clarified to Business Insider that he has no plans to launch a company focused on canine health yet. Rather, Katara will be subjected to a version of the rigorous data collection and longevity interventions that he chronicles in great detail for his millions of followers on X and Instagram. "She's going to become the most measured dog in the world," he said in an interview. "We're going to do a whole bunch of longevity therapies on her because dogs are amazing." based pic.twitter.com/USG6pBGTpG — Talmage Johnson (@talmagejohnson_) August 27, 2026 Johnson thinks there may be relatively straightforward ways to improve dogs' health, starting with food. He said most commercial dog food contains much higher concentrations of harmful compounds. "These are things that glue your organs together," he said. "We're feeding them things that are terrible for their bodies." Dogs and humans are not as different as one might expect, according to Johnson. That means advances in dogs can also help humans. "It's remarkable how much dogs and humans have in common," he said. "When you read through the literature on dogs, and you just replace humans with dogs, there are so many similarities." Johnson has often been frustrated by how long it takes for new human treatments to be approved. That is much less of a problem in animals. "The path for drug approval is substantially faster for dogs than humans, so you can get a lot of scientific work done in a shorter period of time," he said. Several startups are already working to extend dogs' lifespans. Loyal is developing the first FDA-approved longevity and lifespan-extension drugs for dogs , while Rejuvenate Bio is taking a more experimental gene-therapy approach, targeting chronic age-related diseases in animals, such as osteoarthritis, heart disease, and cancer. Johnson does not expect convincing people to improve their dogs' health to be difficult. As someone who urges people to sleep more and avoid alcohol, he has found that many will prioritize their pets' well-being over their own. "Humans will oftentimes care for their dogs better than they'll care for themselves," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I spent my Saturday with the Target exec on a mission to fix its stores
events.summary: Target's chief stores officer, Adrienne Costanzo, is responsible for more than 350,000 workers across 2,000 stores in all 50 US states. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Back-to-school is Target's biggest shopping moment outside of the holidays. Business Insider went behind the scenes with Target's stores chief to see how it's tackling the rush. "This is the 16th state in three weeks of visits," Adrienne Costanzo told us. If the holiday shopping season is a retailer's final exam each year, back-to-school is the midterms . For Target, this year's test is a big one. Success depends on getting the basics right: exciting merchandise, fully stocked stores, and competitive pricing . Those are all areas where Target has stumbled in recent years. This year's season is also an early read on CEO Michael Fiddelke's turnaround plan. He took the reins earlier this year after a rough patch for Target, which faced boycotts in 2025 after winding down several diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Last week, it faced fresh criticism over a children's Halloween costume resembling racist minstrel imagery; Target pulled it and apologized. To see how Target is trying to pull it off, Business Insider visited a pair of stores in Madison, Wisconsin, with chief stores officer Adrienne Costanzo. Costanzo huddles with store manager, Ben Cossack, before her walkthrough. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Costanzo is a 22-year veteran of Target and has held numerous roles in HR and store operations. Her appointment to her current position came in February 2025, roughly six months before Fiddelke was announced as CEO. She's now responsible for more than 350,000 workers across 2,000 stores in all 50 US states. This month, Costanzo has logged serious miles to check in with shoppers, employees, and store managers about what's working and what isn't in their stores as they head back to school. "This is the 16th state in three weeks of visits," she said while in Madison. "I've been to Michigan, I've been to Nebraska, I mean, I've been like everywhere." On the Saturday of this visit, grade-school parents were gearing up for the first day of class, and college students at the University of Wisconsin were kitting out their apartments. Dorm move-ins were still a week away, and both locations were doing brisk business. Shoppers fill the center aisle at a Target store near the University of Wisconsin. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Unlike the holidays, different school seasons peak at different times, creating all manner of complexity for inventory planning and staffing, Fiddelke told investors on a second-quarter earnings call. "The foot traffic is incredible — the parents and students," Costanzo said of her multi-state tour. Her visits include conversations with shoppers who express relief at Target's improved in-stock rates and positive impressions of collaborations with brands like LoveShackFancy and Hollister, she said. It's a return to the sort of merchandising that helps draw customers into stores and tempts them to add unexpected finds to an already full shopping cart. During the tours, Costanzo talked with store managers about everything from their hiring and training efforts in the prior months to a new trailer loading strategy that helps store workers get merchandise onto shelves more quickly. Costanzo talks with employees in the stockroom. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider Even with higher traffic, both locations were more tightly stocked than on previous Business Insider visits, with no inventory carts lingering in the aisles. (Costanzo's visit was announced ahead of time.) A notable exception to the fully stocked shelves was a section reserved for Pokémon, which the store director said sold out after more than 50 customers had been waiting in line for the merchandise to drop. "You can't sell air," Costanzo said, explaining to the store leaders that her team is working on a solution to ensure important shelf space doesn't sit idle while suppliers work to catch up with high demand. Customers shop at a Target store near the University of Wisconsin. Dominick Reuter/Business Insider While this visit involved a bit of an entourage, Costanzo said she also drops in on stores incognito, which allows her to get more of a guest-eye view of how Target's teams are performing. One such visit, she said, showed her Target still has work to do in training and balancing the responsibilities of store teams during busy moments like this. "Our team puts their head down and is doing the work," she said. "I did not experience a lot of the eye contact and smiles. I didn't experience as much as I would have wanted around attention on the check lanes." "I want us to stand at our best when we're busy with the total experience," she added. Have a tip? events.title: Nepal-Tibet floods add to the world's growing natural disaster economic bill
events.summary: After the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods , the focus on natural disasters in the age of climate change has been further magnified. These catastrophes are becoming increasingly deadly and their humanitarian and economic costs are growing – with uncertainty continuing to rise. “Climate change will affect all aspects of human life and the natural world, leading to increasing losses and damages,” analysts at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said. “Lives and livelihoods, as well as the socio-economic stability of countries and entire communities are at risk, along with the natural environment on which we all depend.” Big hits This year alone, there have been 48 recorded natural disasters spanning floods, earthquakes, wildfires, typhoons and windstorms, ReliefWeb data shows. Estimates of economic damage vary depending on what is measured – but they are all stark. Last year was the costliest so far: disasters added up to about $120 billion in economic costs, according to a report by the UK charity Christian Aid, based on estimates by insurer Aon. They were led by the Palisades and Eaton wildfires in Los Angeles in January, which racked up economic losses of more than $60 billion, followed by the tropical cyclones that hit Indonesia, Malaysia, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Vietnam, which cost about $25 billion. The cyclones were made more intense by climate change; they developed over the North Indian Ocean, which was 0.2°C warmer than the historical average from 1991 to 2020 and would have been 1°C cooler without human-caused climate change, analysts at World Weather Attribution and Earth.org said. “The combination of heavy monsoon rains and climate change is a deadly mix,” said Sarah Kew, a climate researcher at the Royal Netherlands Meteorological Institute and lead author of the study. “Monsoon rains are normal in this part of the world. What is not normal is the growing intensity of these storms and how they are affecting millions of people and claiming hundreds of lives.” The Los Angeles wildfires remain the costliest by far. For earthquakes, at the top is the 2011 disaster in Japan's Tohoku province, which also included a tsunami that upwards of $320 billion, while Hurricane Katrina, which hit the US in 2005, is the costliest cyclone, with estimates of more than $200 billion. A 2024 report from the Paris-based International Chamber of Commerce and Belgian economic consultancy Oxera estimated that extreme weather events cost the global economy about $2 trillion from 2014 to 2023, spanning almost 4,000 disasters that affected 1.6 billion people. In 2022 and 2023, those damages hit $451 billion, almost a fifth more than the previous eight years combined. A study by insurer Swiss Re estimated that extreme weather caused $145 billion in insured losses last year. The loss of economic assets is also stark: in the EU, weather and climate-related extremes caused economic losses of assets of about €822 billion ($952.2 billion) from 1980 to 2024, with about a quarter, or more than €208 billion, occurring between 2021 and 2024, the European Environment Agency said. Analysts at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Climate Portal say it is “unfortunately” difficult to pin down the exact or even the estimated cost of climate change's effects on the world economy. “We don’t know. The risks are severe, and grow worse the longer we wait to address them, but climate scientists and economists are very far from agreeing on an exact dollar cost,” they said.

events.title: I moved in with my parents 3 years ago to help my dad with my mom's caregiving. I'm glad I got that time with her.
events.summary: The author moved in with her parents to help with her mother's caregiving. Courtesy of Jeanni Ritchie I moved in with my parents to help my dad with my mom's caregiving. She had dementia, and it kept changing the rules. It was hard at first, but we found a rhythm. I'm so glad we got that time together. I moved back to my Louisiana hometown from Biloxi, Mississippi, in 2023 after 35 years on my own. It was the solution to two problems — I was newly divorced with nowhere to go, and my dad needed help caring for my mom, who had dementia . It was supposed to be temporary. Respite care for him, refuge for me. A year or two, tops. We almost didn't make it through the first six months. It was difficult at first I was angry, hurting, and trying to figure out what came next. Moving back home felt strangely familiar, like being a teenager again. Unfortunately, I acted like one sometimes, too. My mom and I struggled during those first months. I was trying to help, but she didn't want my help. And while my dad appreciated the extra hands, he often found himself caught in the middle. I understood dementia intellectually, but emotionally, I felt rejected by my own mother. The author and her parents found a rhythm living together. Courtesy of Jeanni Ritchie We would make agreements about things like laundry schedules and a carved-out office space for me. I would carefully follow Mom's wishes, but dementia often made them null and void. Mom would forget our conversations and become frustrated when things weren't the way she remembered. The laundry room became our biggest battleground. If my clothes were in the washer, she would often become upset and insist she had "lost her house." The clothes weren't really the issue. Dementia was changing the rules, and the laundry room became the place where she most clearly felt she was no longer fully in control of her own home. It didn't matter that I was her daughter; it felt as though another woman had moved into her space, and dementia made it difficult to understand I was there to help. It took time, but I learned the new rules of the house Over time, I learned to navigate Mom's unspoken cues and emotional needs. A closed bedroom door meant she needed space. An open door often meant it was a good day. I became a quiet pair of hands in the background, lightening the physical load. I learned when the kitchen fairy needed to sneak in after everyone was asleep to preserve Mom's dignity. Most importantly, I stopped taking everything personally. For someone who had spent a lifetime wearing her heart on her sleeve, that was no small lesson. My mind had always understood dementia , but it took time for my heart to catch up. Over time, the author began to see caregiving as a gift. Courtesy of Jeanni Ritchie During my second year back home, I began to understand the power of co-regulation. I had healed from the aftermath of my divorce , and I was experiencing a joy I had not known in years. It was spreading throughout the house. The progression of dementia didn't stop, but the atmosphere in our home changed. There was more laughter, more music, more outings, and more happiness woven into our everyday routines. Dad and I became true caregiving partners. He felt comfortable accepting overnight assignments at work while I was at home with Mom, and I was able to travel when I needed a break from caregiving . I'd do all the cooking and cleaning, even stocking the refrigerator with cooked meals before traveling. I did the grocery shopping and ran errands. The trade-off was open bank access, a gas card, and a travel credit card. I didn't have to worry about money; Dad didn't have to worry about Mom. It became our permanent plan By the third year, this temporary solution was working so well that it became our permanent plan. Caregiving didn't feel like a burden to me. It felt like a gift. For years, I regretted my rebellious teenage years and taking my parents for granted. I was given an unexpected do-over — a chance to spend time with them, help care for them, and repay some small portion of what they've poured into my life. The author and her dad leaned on each other while caregiving for her mom. Courtesy of Jeanni Ritchie I'd laughingly sing "Cinderelly, Cinderelly" while I cleaned the house and cooked meals, but I also got to live Cinderella's life after the ball. By not having household living expenses, I was able to travel. I got to go on long-awaited adventures, and we all got a little bit of breathing room. When I was home, Mom and I enjoyed theatre productions and movies together, and she became somewhat of a local celebrity when she'd appear in videos of our adventures. When I traveled, I'd leave "surprise boxes" for her. Sometimes they had small gifts to open each day. Other times there were cards to be opened each morning, each carefully dated and filled with funny cartoon clips or a heartfelt memory inside. When she and Dad traveled , I'd use the time to deep clean the house, reorganize the kitchen cabinets and return things to their proper places, or just rest. When we grew frustrated or worried, Dad and I had each other to lean on. When one of us got angry, the other took the role of confidant and comforter. That was perhaps the greatest tag-team benefit of all. Dad and I knew there might come a day when we'd need to recalibrate as the disease progressed. Dementia continued to change the rules, but we'd chosen to enjoy each season as it came. One week into a planned seven-week road trip, I got a call from my sister. Mom had a massive stroke and would not survive. I drove straight home, and we spent the next nine days by her bedside. Her best friend told us that she'd confided in her that, as much as she hated what dementia was doing to her mind, the last year had been the happiest of her entire life. I had to hold on to those words as she was lowered into the ground. Dementia might have taken some of her memories, but it couldn't take the love. Caregiving for her became one of the greatest honors we could've had. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tax promises, defence targets and Iran: Andy Burnham’s budget headaches
events.summary: As economic circumstances worsen, the PM’s commitments have left him and the chancellor in a tight spot When Andy Burnham made his first speech after returning as an MP, he promised that as prime minister he would oversee “the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years”. His style, direction and communication has been a big shift from Keir Starmer’s approach, but as he heads into the autumn, the new prime minister faces some very similar problems. With an early budget in late October , and worsening economic circumstances, Burnham has made promises and commitments that put him in a tight spot. Here are some of the constraints over the coming months that Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, must contend with in their autumn budget. 1. Fiscal rules The biggest risk of Burnham as prime minister was always whether he would spook the bond markets and set in train a Liz Truss-style meltdown. Starmer’s allies often played up this fear but there is no doubt that Burnham had to ensure that markets knew he was a serious operator. Gilt yields rose after an interview last year in which he said the government was “in hock to the bond markets” . So, Burnham has committed to Rachel Reeves’s fiscal rules on debt and borrowing, though he has indicated he will “use, obviously, any flexibility within them” where he can borrow to fund further investment. 2. Tax promises Burnham has said he will “stick to the manifesto”, which promises no increases in income tax, national insurance or VAT, though he cautioned in an interview earlier this week that the public needed to be “realistic” about what needed to be funded and how difficult more spending would be. That decision to stick to no rises in personal taxation had left businesses fearing a tax raid – and Burnham has been urged by some leftwing and union leaders to consider further wealth taxes. But the prime minister told the FT this week he was loth to do more to increase the costs of doing business and did not want to target “wealth creators”. With each utterance, the possibilities of revenue raisers become ever narrower. Burnham hinted in the past that he hoped to unfreeze the personal allowance, which would amount to a tax cut, but has recently been more cautious about this because of the costs. 3. Economic turmoil Reeves left £23.6bn of “headroom” in her last budget, which gives Healey a buffer to meet the fiscal rule of balancing day-to-day spending with receipts. But the Iran war and subsequent rises in inflation and borrowing costs for servicing Britain’s national debt, which is now almost £3tn, are likely to have an effect on that headroom. Treasury sources say the impact may not be as much as feared, but with the strait of Hormuz remaining closed, growth is sluggish and inflation creeping upwards. 4. Cost of living Burnham has made a number of popular early interventions to help ease the cost of living. Some, such as cutting VAT on energy bills, are ostensibly funded by cutting existing programmes such as the digital ID scheme, though, as the former minister Darren Jones pointed out, that was never properly costed in the first place. Healey has suggested there are no further plans to offer energy support at this October price cap, though prices have risen by 4%, wiping out the impact of the VAT cut. The Treasury will want a contingency plan in place in case more help is needed in January – probably a targeted scheme for more vulnerable households. The Resolution Foundation has suggested that even a targeted scheme for those earning under £25k would cost about £2bn. 5. Defence targets The Treasury confirmed on Friday that it would delay setting out when the UK would meet the target of spending 3% of GDP on defence, until next year’s spending review. Healey’s budget to duck setting a date for 3% defence spending target Read more Burnham would have had to find an additional £4.7bn over five years for defence in October’s budget, after Starmer announced £15bn extra when he published the defence investment plan, without saying where the cash would come from. The remaining £10.3bn will also have to be raised by “reallocating budget” from across government departments. Healey resigned as defence secretary in June under Starmer’s leadership, accusing the then prime minister of being “unable” and the Treasury “unwilling” to “commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country”. Labour has committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by the middle of the next decade. But there will be endless pressure to go faster, putting more and more of a squeeze on other departmental budgets. 6. Public control Burnham promised he wanted to place life’s essentials “back under public control” – specifically Thames Water. In June, he told the Guardian he favoured public ownership for Thames Water, which is struggling with a £20bn debt.

events.title: Reality check for China’s carmakers as authorities tell them to focus on quality, not tech
events.summary: Vice-minister says that to ensure safety, new technologies that fail to pass stricter approval procedures will be barred from market A nationwide inspection campaign assessing the quality of Chinese-made cars that was announced this week would see some consumers shelve purchase plans, exacerbating a bearish outlook for the country’s auto sector, dealers and analysts said. Vice-Minister of Industry and Information Technology Xin Guobin told a news conference in Beijing on Wednesday that new auto products and technologies would be barred from entering the market unless they passed stricter approval procedures. “Some reckless innovative designs were installed in vehicles without sufficient testing and verification,” Xin said. “Several incidents attracted public attention due to concerns about the cars’ quality and the safety of autonomous driving technology.” “Several accidents and growing consumer complaints have spurred the regulators into action,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “With improved oversight, carmakers will have to shift their focus from making their vehicles more intelligent to ensuring quality.”

events.title: How to make a bestseller: insiders reveal the tricks of the book trade
events.summary: From cover design to shelf placement and influencer partnerships … how publishers will persuade you to buy their books this autumn Think about the last book you bought. How did you choose it? Was it from a recommendation, a review, a TikTok video? Did the cover grab you, were you swayed by the quotes on the front, or did you just happen to spot it on an appealing table as you walked into the shop? Did you think about all the nudges that led you to that decision – by the publisher, the bookseller or that person you follow on Insta? The reality is that our reading choices are directed and massaged at every turn. “It’s all about the art of persuasion,” says Philip Gwyn Jones, who was a publisher for more than 30 years and is now a literary agent. And who are the persuaders? They’re the booksellers, the supermarket stock buyers, the publishing houses and their ranks of marketers and publicists. And, more recently, persuasion often comes from BookTokers and online influencers, social media videos, podcasts and Instagram posts. How is all this changing publishing? We all judge books to some extent by their covers, but did you know how much thought goes into finding just the right cover, colour, font and design? These covers are focus-grouped, shown to supermarket buyers and often changed at their behest, according to Jamie Keenan, one of Britain’s leading book designers. “That happens quite a lot,” he says. “If Tesco with commercial books, or Waterstones with literary stuff, don’t like it, they’ve got a tremendous amount of clout.” (Waterstones and Tesco declined to speak to me for this piece.) Meanwhile, online browsing and buying have brought about big changes. “There’s been a move towards more iconic book covers because of thumbnail images [on apps and websites],” Keenan explains. “One very simple emblem or logo that you can see from a distance, even when it’s two inches tall. Nice bright colours and big type,” he adds. “That’s what publishers are doing to attract people’s attention.” It’s true: when I went into Waterstones last week, I felt like reaching for my sunglasses to shield the glare of garish, saturated colours screaming from the fiction shelves: more sweet shop than book store. When I shared a photo on Instagram, a number of authors messaged me. “I hate it,” said one (whose own latest novel has a brightly coloured cover). “It’s just so brash.” Yet ironically, because all these books look the same, the effect is to make them blend in, not stand out. “Jewel tones have the industry in a headlock,” messaged another. And then there are the increasing numbers of copycat covers, so that every cosy crime novel suddenly looks like Richard Osman’s bestsellers – cream background, coloured border, hand-lettering – and all heartwarming Japanese books have to feature a cat. (At his last publishing house, says Gwyn Jones, for Japanese fiction “there was this unspoken imperative to put a cat on the cover even if there wasn’t a major role for a cat in the book. It did seem to make a difference.”) “You quite often get briefs on what are called comparable titles,” Keenan says. “That’s a nod-and-a-wink way of saying, ‘Can you do something that looks a bit like these three?’” After the cover does its trick, we read the publisher’s description on the back. That’s the work of copywriters. “The cover designer has got them to pick up the book,” says a copywriter for a major commercial publisher. “It’s my job to make sure they don’t put it down again.” The blurb is how we decide if this book is one for us. “You’ve got seconds to grab people,” says the copywriter. One of their tricks is to use Christopher Booker’s book The Seven Basic Plots . “Most stories can fit into three or four of Booker’s categories: The Quest, Overcoming the Monster and so on. It gives you tools to tell the story of the book in different ways. You want to say: ‘It’s the same but different.’” What if an author isn’t writing what’s on trend right now? “For the best part of two decades,” the copywriter says, “we had Scandi noir: very dark, psychological thrillers. Now cosy crime is absolutely everything. If a writer is still writing noir and wants their books to be in the supermarkets, it needs to look like the books that are selling in supermarkets.” That means “you’ll find books being packaged rather differently to how they [really] are”. These cosy crime blurbs need to, frankly, make death and violence sound like a minor inconvenience, so they focus on the mystery aspect (the books are “ingenious”, full of “twists and turns”) or the welcoming narrative tone (“delicious’” and “delightful”) or the sense of tradition they follow as “quintessentially British” stories. But “publishers are lemmings,” the copywriter says, “and that’s where the market is.” “There has been a sense since the mid-2000s that popular fiction readers’ tastes have narrowed,” they continue, “following one or two big trends. That parallels [the rise of] social media.

events.title: Trump claims US will take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has said Washington is making an unprecedented push to take control of about a fifth of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, claiming it will provide relief to Americans' pain amid soaring energy prices. The “biggest oil deal in world history” would give the US control over more than 65 billion barrels of crude, Mr Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday. He said the “historic transaction” was being co-ordinated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez “through a partnership with private business”. No details were provided, including which oilfields and companies are involved, or how the US would exercise control. Reuters reported that the fields are in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions. It is also unclear if the agreement would face legal or regulatory challenges, particularly in Venezuela. Neither Washington nor Caracas have not released any official statement related to Mr Trump's announcement. Venezuela has the world's largest proven reserves of crude oil with more than 303 billion barrels, accounting for about 17 per cent of global supply. Mr Trump claimed the agreement “more than doubles American oil reserves, greatly increases our oil supply, and will substantially lower gas prices for all Americans, long into the future, while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course towards tremendous success and great prosperity”. Inflation has remained elevated in the US and gas prices have soared by as much as 50 per cent amid its war on Iran, drawing the ire of American consumers and causing Mr Trump's approval ratings to reach historic lows. “This transaction will greatly strengthen the already growing relationship between Venezuela and the United States,” Mr Trump said. The apparent agreement comes after weeks-long negotiations between Washington and Caracas over another deal that would give American companies long-term access to a group of Venezuelan oilfields and guarantee the resulting crude supply to the US. Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week granting new oil exploration and production rights to several companies, particularly US firms. It also comes after US operatives captured former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, in a move the White House said would usher in a new political and economic era in the South American country. At that time, Mr Trump claimed that interim Venezuelan authorities would turn over 30 million to 50 million barrels of “sanctioned” oil to the US. Shortly after that, Mr Trump pushed for the world's largest oil companies to invest $100 billion in Venezuela.

events.title: Households could save up to £173 a year by switching to fixed energy deal
events.summary: Moving tariffs will cushion the blow from the October price cap rise and the increase widely predicted for January With higher energy bills looming and warnings of worse to come in the new year, many households could save up to £173 a year by switching to a fixed deal. Millions of households in Great Britain will face the highest energy charges in three years after it was announced that the government’s price cap will rise again in October. This will be the second increase in three months. However, moving to a fixed tariff would enable people to avoid this increase and one that has been widely predicted for January. These tariffs offer a set standing charge and unit costs for a certain period; often one or two years. Gas and electricity prices will rise by 4% from 1 October under the new cap, after climbing 13% at the start of July. This will take the rate for 22 million households on default tariffs to the equivalent of £1,723 a year, based on typical gas and electricity usage, and will kick in just as many people will probably be turning the heating back on. However, even the energy regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem , has gone into Martin Lewis mode, extolling the money-saving benefits offered by a fixed tariff. “Savings are available by choosing a fixed tariff, which are available at £100 or more below the October price cap,” it says. About 11m homes (35% of the total) are already on fixed tariffs and will not be affected by the rise announced this week. They will be protected from price increases until their current deal comes to an end. Price comparison websites say many households could save decent sums by switching to one of the cheapest fixed energy tariffs on the market. Doing a quick check using one of these sites will show you what is available for your household based on your personal usage. At the time of writing there were plenty of fixed energy deals available that beat the new October figure, “offering households certainty over what they’ll pay through the coldest months, regardless of what happens to wholesale prices”, says Uswitch.com. The cheapest is a fixed tariff from Fuse Energy priced at £1,550 a year for a typical-usage home – which is £173 below the October cap figure, and £113 below the current cap. This deal is available in various forms: there is one that lasts for 14 months – Fuse Energy August 2026 Fixed (14m) V1 – being offered by Uswitch and Confused.com, as well as Fuse Energy itself. Meanwhile, MoneySuperMarket offers a version of it that is fixed for 18 months, called Fuse Energy August 2026 Fixed (18m) V10. There are several other fixed deals available from suppliers including Co-op Energy, Octopus Energy, E.ON Next and Ecotricity that offer people typical savings (versus the October price cap) of more than £100 a year. Some of these deals are exclusive to one or more comparison sites but in many cases you can get them direct from the supplier. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The advice to consider switching to a fixed tariff has been given extra weight by the prediction that the pain is only going to get worse. According to analysts at Cornwall Insight, bills are forecast to rise by a further 9% in January, just when temperatures may be at their lowest. If that happens, the typical household bill will climb by £149 to about £1,872 a year. However, the January 2027 figure will not be confirmed until November, and a lot could happen between now and then. Before you switch, you will need to check how long remains on your contract and whether there are any exit fees, says Gareth Kloet at Go.Compare. October’s cap would have been even higher if the government had not announced a temporary VAT cut on domestic electricity. This will reduce the tax from 5% to zero between 1 October this year and 31 March 2027, resulting in a £45 a year saving for a typical household (this has been reflected in the new cap). The VAT cut will benefit those currently on fixed tariffs as well as those whose bills are pegged to the price cap – the discount will be automatically applied to people’s accounts by suppliers. Many suppliers offer tariffs with cheaper electricity to smart meter customers for power consumed outside of peak times, says Ofgem, so it is worth asking about those. Because the price cap is based on typical usage, aside from shopping around for a better deal, the best way to keep bills under control is to cut your energy use wherever possible. You may want to check to see if you qualify for help, says Sarah Coles at the investment platform AJ Bell. Initiatives include the warm home discount scheme , which will reopen in October and is a one-off £150 discount off your electricity bill.

events.title: UK risks falling behind in AI race without faster telecoms upgrades, say executives
events.summary: Planning delays and slow 5G upgrades could leave the UK unable to cope with a surge in AI-related traffic The UK risks becoming a laggard in the global AI race as crucial telecoms upgrades to harness the technology fall behind rival nations, according to senior industry executives. The infrastructure AI race has centred on the need to build datacentres , and to ensure they have access to the huge water and energy supplies required to cool and supply the computational power to train and run AI models. However, as adoption spreads, the UK’s broadband and mobile networks will be expected to carry an immense volume of AI-related traffic produced by consumers and businesses. While the UK has addressed its previously embarrassing status of having one of the slowest broadband speeds in Europe , as BT’s Openreach and other service providers cover the country with full-fibre connections, efforts to upgrade the nation’s 5G mobile networks are not keeping pace. Mobile coverage in the UK is worse than any of the 27 EU member states , and every other member of the G7, according to a recent report by the consumer group Which? based on data from Opensignal. According to the analysis, the UK ranks 57th globally for network performance, 70th for download speeds and 55th for the reliable quality needed for activities such as video calls, streaming and gaming. “If with the technology and services we use today [networks] are sub-optimal, imagine when you add mass AI usage and other associated activities,” said Andrea Donà, networks director at VodafoneThree, the UK’s largest mobile operator. “I would go further. I am embarrassed today at the level of quality of our network[s]. The UK is worthy of what EE, O2 and VodafoneThree can offer, but we need reform.” Highlighting the risks of an AI-traffic crunch, Donà likened the situation to consumers suffering signal loss at a big public event – such as a gig at Wembley, the British grand prix at Silverstone, or a rugby international at Twickenham. “What we see now only with a mass aggregation of people is a proxy, an indication of the things that will come. That [one-off] experience will be constant because of the additional capacity [consumers] will need in an AI world.” Another senior telecoms executive said that while the issue of AI and connectivity is now “nascent”, it is going to become a “national competitiveness issue” in the way the slow rollout of full-fibre broadband did. “Things are going to change massively with the next wave of devices, in two or three years when AI is integrated into everything,” he said. “AI companies, and governments, don’t think about networks, but they will when they hold them back.” The UK’s main mobile operators are investing heavily in important 5G stand-alone technology – VodafoneThree has committed £11bn to upgrade masts – but the industry says it is being held back by issues including planning delays. Donà said that it is not about needing to build more sites, in VodafoneThree’s case it is actually reducing its nationwide network of masts by 30%, but the restrictive regulations to simply upgrade existing sites. About 96% of the upgrades VodafoneThree need to make are on existing sites, but more than half of those will require some form of planning permission, which companies say can be a lengthy and bureaucratic process. “Andy Burnham has his agenda on growth,” said Donà. “Our infrastructure is here to help the government and UK economy. Planning reform is the lowest possible cost growth policy – it doesn’t require any government money. It could be a great first 100 days-win for the new prime minister.” Mobile operators also argue that despite their networks being classified as critical national infrastructure – such as datacentres and energy and water systems – they do not receive the reliefs that the government has offered those sectors in areas such as business rates and energy.

events.title: Sovereignty, farming and fishing: Iceland votes on its future with the EU
events.summary: Country holds a knife-edge referendum that cuts across political divides on taking step closer to Brussels after Trump threats towards Greenland For a long time, the prospect of becoming the third generation to run his family farm was an exciting one, says Davíð Clausen Pétursson. Icelandic farmers were starting to get higher prices for their meat and milk, debt was no longer an occupational prerequisite and innovation was on the rise. Now the 29-year-old is anxiously awaiting the result of a referendum on Saturday, when Icelanders will be asked whether or not they want to restart accession talks with the EU. Davíð believes joining the bloc could have negative ramifications for farmers all over Iceland, slowing down progress made in the sector and reducing profits. Across Europe small and medium-sized farms have struggled, with thousands closing each year because of brutal economic circumstances. In Iceland, however, the picture has been somewhat brighter for some farmers who have been able to make a profit and innovate. Since the government announced that it was bringing forward the planned vote, amid Donald Trump’s efforts to take control of neighbouring Greenland , debate has taken in everything from food security to national identity, defence, housing, inflation, language, and natural resources. The latest polls show the two sides – which cut across the political spectrum and generations – are neck and neck. According to Thursday’s Gallup poll, the no campaign is slightly in the lead with 51.6% of the vote and yes at 48.4%. While the yes campaign has strong support, critics of the EU have in some ways been louder in part because a yes vote is less decisive: it is agreeing to begin negotiations, not saying yes to joining the EU. “Of course I am quite invested in how it goes,” says Davíð at his remote farm in Hvammur, south-west Iceland, overlooked by a mountain that features in the Icelandic sagas. “I want at least to build my life around farming for the next 30-40 years and I would also like my kids to be able to do that as well. I am just not sure that it will be possible if we go that route.” He says a “yes” win would lead to the years of negotiations before the nation votes again on any deal reached, and he fears the resulting uncertainty would put a halt to all the progress and the momentum in farming. Then, they would have to deal with the repercussions of the outcome, where he fears farmers’ interests, drowned out by the more valuable and noisier fishing lobby, would not be prioritised. As Davíð explained to his nine-year-old son – the vote has been a big talking point at school – a litre of milk currently costs them about 100 ISK to produce, which they can sell for 145 ISK. He worries that joining the EU would mean he would have to significantly decrease the price of his milk and other products. “It is not that I am against anything in the EU at all. I am half Danish, my mother is Danish and we of course buy a lot from Europe ,” he says. “The regulations they have there are suitable for countries that live next to each other, but I am fearful that if it is a yes, the uncertainty will make it quite hard for us to see where we are going, so that will put everything at a bit of a halt.” Iceland’s current farming system was built on the country being a lone independent state in the Atlantic with unique weather conditions, he says. “We can figure it out ourselves. We make trade agreements with everyone around us, we try to take off the tariffs and have free trade with the products we really need, we put tariffs on the products we are trying to produce here.” He understands that high food costs are frustrating for consumers, but believes it is worth it. “There is a high cost to food security in Iceland. But there is an even bigger cost to losing that and being dependent.” The EU vote taps into a sense of lament among some in Iceland that in a globalised, highly connected world the country’s foundation in agriculture and fishing – central to life there until a few decades ago – is being rapidly forgotten. Davíð says that 30 years ago children came to work on the farm in the summer, but machinery and specialisation mean that is no longer possible. Sigurrós Birta Jóhannsdóttir, 22, visited the farm on an educational visit with a coach load of other agriculture students. Jóhannsdóttir, who works on a farm that she will take over in the future, will be voting no on Saturday because she believes that negotiations will only slow down progress and cost money. Supporters believe joining the EU could help bring down the high cost of living and inflation in Iceland, and would be good for the country’s security. At his home by the sea in Þorlákshöfn, Kári Böðvarsson, 79, says he plans to vote yes, despite being right-leaning politically. “It doesn’t matter if you’re on the right or on the left, what your opinion is, people are just voting across politics,” the retired fisher says.

events.title: ‘Winter panic’: EU gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years
events.summary: As one of Europe’s biggest consumers of gas the UK may be particularly exposed to heightened price volatility Europe is on course to enter the cooler months with gas stores at their lowest level in 13 years, which has triggered “winter panic” among energy traders, experts have warned. The EU’s gas stocks were 63% full in the last week of August, well below the 80% average for late August over recent years and among the lowest levels ever recorded for this time of year. At the current sluggish rate of gas storage injections, the EU is likely to enter the winter heating season with gas stocks about a fifth below the five-year average, and at their lowest level since 2013, according to Greg Molnar, a gas analyst and professor. “Low storage levels are naturally increasing the risk of heightened winter price volatility,” he said, which could be made worse by “cold spells or slow wind patterns” increasing gas usage over the winter. The UK may be particularly exposed to market volatility, because it is one of the biggest gas consumers in Europe but has some of the lowest levels of domestic gas storage capacity. Typically, the UK relies on imports of gas via pipeline from Europe or tankers from the US and the Middle East. Chris O’Shea, chief executive of the British Gas owner Centrica , said this week the UK had “almost no gas in storage” for the coming winter. The EU’s gas stores have struggled to rise towards a watered-down target of 80% full by the start of winter, since the US-Israel war on Iran triggered severe disruption to exports of oil and gas from the Gulf region. A cold end to last winter, and higher-than-usual gas power generation during Europe’s heatwaves this summer, have also contributed to the bloc’s depleted gas stores. In a typical year, owners of storage facilities fill them up during the summer when both demand and prices are lower. Europe’s gas market prices have “stayed relatively calm” this summer in the hope that the strait of Hormuz would be reopened and winter stocks could be rebuilt. However, “no one expects it to happen any time soon”, according to Bjarne Schieldrop, chief analyst commodities at the Nordic banking group SEB. “As a result, the European natural gas market has run into a bit of a winter panic over the past week,” Schieldrop added. Although Europe is not expected to experience physical shortages of gas this winter, traders expect higher prices. Benchmark gas price has climbed to three-year highs above €68 per megawatt-hour (MWh) in recent weeks, more than double the price at the start of the year. Prices have risen sharply on the growing expectation that market traders in the EU will need to compete with Asian buyers to secure cargoes of liquefied natural gas as temperatures begin to cool. Without a return of gas exports from the Middle East, Europe’s benchmark price “would likely need to move above €100/MWh” to attract enough shipments of gas to meet winter demand, according to analysts at Goldman Sachs. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Gas supply concerns are particularly acute in western Europe, where storage levels are well below those in countries such as Italy and Poland, which have managed to top up their gas stores to over 80% full. In Germany, which has Europe’s largest gas storage capacity, facilities are about half-full, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe. Storage levels in Belgium and the Netherlands, which connect directly to the UK gas market via gas pipelines, stand at 51% and 45%. The UK’s reliance on global gas imports is expected to deepen as declining gas production from the UK’s North Sea sector accelerates, and Norwegian output begins to fall from 2030. The government is considering plans to provide direct financial support to safeguard domestic gas infrastructure, after an official consultation found that homes and businesses risk running out of gas within the next decade , despite its growing clean energy sources. This could include offering financial support to the owners of gas storage facilities and pipeline operators, to make it economically viable to upgrade and maintain them in the decades ahead. The UK energy regulator, Ofgem, said this week that typical gas and electricity bills will rise by 4% from October under its quarterly cap, after climbing 13% at the start of July, to take account of global energy market price rises caused by the war on Iran.

events.title: Meta’s $18 billion settlement puts TikTok and YouTube on notice. Who's next on the firing line?
events.summary: Meta's $18 billion settlement in the social media addiction trial has shifted focus to other platforms. Under the settlement conditions, Meta called on YouTube and TikTok to also make changes to their apps. California's Attorney General Rob Bonta told CNBC he has plans to target other big players next. Meta 's watershed social media trial just wrapped up in California, but now attention is shifting to the wider industry with TikTok, YouTube and Snap next on the firing line. The Instagram and Facebook owner settled in week two of a trial brought by a coalition of tens of U.S. states alleging that the tech giant had misled the public about the harms its platforms posed to younger users. The agreement includes a payment of up to $18 billion , part of which is tied to conditional action by other social media giants. Meta said it would also make fundamental changes to its platforms for users under the age of 18, including but not limited to a 2-hour daily usage limit that only a parent can lift, disabling extreme makeup and cosmetic surgery filters, tighter age verification measures, and night mode. Meta said it would only pay 70% of the settlement , or around $12.7 billion to the states over a period of 10-years. The remaining $5.3 billion is conditional on the company's rivals TikTok and Alphabet 's YouTube also making similar changes to their apps for younger users. California's Attorney General Rob Bonta, a co-lead in this case alongside New Jersey, Colorado, and Kentucky, said Meta's settlement "gives notice to others in the industry that we're not done, and we expect similar outcomes from them as well." "No company wants what Meta faced in Oakland," Rob Lalka, a professor of practice in management at Tulane University and author of "The Venture Alchemists: How Big Tech Turned Profits Into Power," told CNBC. "I'd expect TikTok, YouTube, and Snapchat to make changes before they ever face that scene. These platforms depend entirely on being trusted, by parents, by users, by advertisers, and the settlement reflects a business decision about reputational risk, which now the boards of these other companies must also make," Lalka added. CNBC has contacted YouTube, TikTok and Snap for comment. Social media giants were already facing increased pressure this year as governments worldwide consider enforcing teen social media bans . Meanwhile, Meta, TikTok, YouTube and Snap have faced a litany of lawsuits. Meta and YouTube lost in a social media addiction trial in Los Angeles earlier this year, which was brought by a plaintiff who claimed her mental health was damaged by addictive features like autoplay and infinite scrolling. Meta also lost a separate social-media case brought by New Mexico Attorney General Raul Torrez , after a court found that the company violated the state's child-safety laws and ordered it to pay over $900 million in penalties. Now that the Meta case has been settled, California's Bonta said, "We'll be continuing our fight across social media," by pursuing lawsuits against the big players like TikTok, Snap and YouTube. In an interview with CNBC on Thursday, Bonta said he approved of Meta calling out other platforms in the settlement. "That is appropriate. This is something that requires an industry-wide solution." He explained that the state of California is currently pursuing active litigation against TikTok. "We are suing TikTok now so we are looking to ensure that they adopt the similar practices and commitments that Meta did, and we are very interested in Snap and YouTube as well," Bonta said. Bonta, New York's Attorney General Letitia James, and 14 other state attorneys filed a lawsuit against TikTok in 2024 for violating consumer protection laws. They said that TikTok harms younger users with addictive features that maximize the amount of time they spend on the platform. The case is ongoing. Bonta added that the state is in communication with Snap, and is pursuing conversations with TikTok, with hopes that YouTube will also come to the table. While Meta is attempting to frame itself as a leader on online youth safety, it neglected those issues for years, according to Lalka. "Let's be clear about how we got here. It took attorneys general stepping in after the harm was already done, because Congress never passed a law to prevent it. "These new rules didn't come from elected policymakers, they were negotiated in a settlement with the company being regulated, and Meta is seeking to ensure its competitors will face the same rules," Lalka said.
