events.title: China’s commercial space sector expands global footprint with Thailand deal
events.summary: GalaxySpace describes mission as first turnkey satellite export to a Southeast Asian customer by a Chinese commercial space company Beijing-based GalaxySpace’s deployed what it called China’s first turnkey satellite export to Southeast Asia this week, underscoring the country’s efforts to boost its influence in the space industry overseas amid competition with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. GalaxySpace said it launched the Lingzhi-09 Thailand CubeSat aboard a Long March-6C rocket – alongside six other satellites – from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Centre in Shanxi province on Tuesday. Developed for Thailand’s Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (GISTDA), the CubeSat satellite will collect remote-sensing data for land, agriculture and ecological applications, and also support practical training for Thai university students. The mission marked the first time that a Chinese commercial space company had developed, launched and deployed a complete satellite in orbit for a Southeast Asian customer as a packaged solution, showing the sector’s ability to provide integrated services spanning satellite delivery, operations and training, the company said. GalaxySpace, China’s first commercial space sector unicorn – a start-up valued at US$1 billion or more – provided GISTDA with an integrated package covering the spacecraft, ground system and personnel training. Thai personnel were trained in China, while GalaxySpace later sent teams to Thailand to help build and test the ground system, it said. Chinese commercial space companies were moving from “exporting products” towards “exporting services and ecosystems”, turning satellite technology into an end-to-end service offering for overseas markets, said Yang Kuan, an associate professor at Beijing Institute of Technology and deputy director of its Institute of Aerospace Policy and Law, in an interview with the Beijing-based Financial News. The overseas push comes as China’s commercial space sector ramps up satellite constellation deployment and overseas expansion in a challenge to SpaceX’s Starlink project.

events.title: SK Hynix starts construction of $5 billion memory hub in US state of Indiana
events.summary: (From left) Indiana Governor Mike Braun, SK Hynix CEO and president Kwak Noh-jung and Purdue University president Mitchell Daniels Jr at the ground-breaking ceremony on Aug 27. SK Hynix is building a $5 billion advanced memory packaging plant in Indiana, expected to open in 2028 and produce next-generation high-bandwidth memory by 2029. The US Chips and Science Act funds the project to strengthen domestic AI chip supply chains and reduce reliance on overseas semiconductor production. The facility will create about 7,000 jobs, collaborate with Purdue University on research, and support former US Forces Korea veterans with new career opportunities. WEST LAFAYETTE, Indiana – SK Hynix held a ground-breaking ceremony on Aug 27 for its advanced memory packaging facility in the US state of Indiana, marking a milestone in Washington’s expansive campaign to rebuild domestic supply chains and manufacturing for strategically important sectors. The West Lafayette plant, costing more than US$4 billion (S$5.08 billion) and occupying a 54ha site, will be SK Hynix’s first high-bandwidth memory (HBM) packaging base in the US. Its clean room is expected to open by October 2028, with mass production of next-generation HBM scheduled to begin in the second half of 2029, chief executive Kwak Noh-jung said at the event . When fully operational, it will be a major HBM hub employing about 1,000 people, he said. HBM is an indispensable part of the global artificial intelligence hardware boom, as it is a prerequisite for assembling Nvidia’s most advanced AI acceleration systems. That has helped SK Hynix grow to become South Korea’s second most valuable company, right behind Samsung Electronics, which has also been lifted by runaway demand for HBM and other memory products. The Indiana project is backed by the US Chips and Science Act , a signature law signed by former president Joe Biden in 2022 that allowed for the South Korean chipmaker to receive as much as US$458 million in direct funding and up to US$500 million in loans. A semiconductor chip on display at the ground-breaking event hosted by SK Hynix and Purdue University. The programme was designed to reduce US dependence on overseas semiconductor production and bring critical chip manufacturing, packaging and research capabilities to American soil. At the event, Kwak said the plant would help strengthen a domestic AI chip supply chain in the US that Washington views as essential to economic and national security. “We will expand our investments and collaboration in the US, grow together, and become the most trusted partner in shaping the future of AI in America,” he said. The Indiana investment is particularly significant because it targets a weak link in the US semiconductor supply chain: advanced packaging. The technology combines multiple chips into a single package, often stacking them vertically to boost performance, as conventional tech miniaturisation approaches become increasingly difficult. Wafers produced by SK Hynix in South Korea will be shipped to Indiana for packaging and testing before being supplied to US customers, the company said. The project is expected to create about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs through construction, operations and related industries. SK Hynix is currently considering more than 100 companies to supply materials, components and equipment, potentially creating a broader semiconductor cluster. SK Hynix also signed an agreement with nearby Purdue University to cooperate on HBM, system integration and advanced packaging research. An advanced packaging research and development test bed will be built alongside the production lines. Reflecting Indiana’s historic ties with South Korea – the state sent about 140,000 troops to the Korean War – parent SK Group also said it would provide new employment and career opportunities for former US Forces Korea service members. events.title: Most Asian stocks advance as attention turns to US Fed chief Kevin Warsh’s speech
events.summary: Traders are hoping US Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh’s speech at the annual meeting of central bankers and economic leaders will give them an insight into decision-makers’ thinking. HONG KONG – Asian stocks mostly rose on Aug 28 ahead of a closely watched speech by US Federal Reserve chief Kevin Warsh, as investors look out for clues about the outlook for interest rates amid elevated inflation and no sign of an end to the Middle East crisis. With the euphoria following Nvidia’s blistering earnings report petering out, the attention is back on the economy as debate surrounds if or when the US central bank will tighten monetary policy. The July Fed meeting saw policymakers keep borrowing costs on hold, but with three of them dissenting in favour of a hike, and, while the latest figures showed inflation easing slightly, it remains well above the 2 per cent target. Worries that price rises will remain elevated for some time – fuelled largely by a spike in energy costs caused by the Iran war – have put upward pressure on long-term Treasury yields, making government borrowing increasingly expensive. Traders are hoping Warsh’s speech at the annual meeting of central bankers and economic leaders at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, will give them an insight into decision-makers’ thinking. However, his last major public appearance after the July meeting was widely panned as giving an ambiguous message, and analysts warn that his refusal to give forward guidance will likely mean investors are left disappointed. Stephen Innes of Quintex Intel said the address – Warsh’s first since taking the helm at the Fed – was “the most consequential central bank speech left this year”, and comes almost three weeks before the next policy announcement. “Recent data has reduced the immediate need for tighter policy, giving Warsh room to re-establish the Fed’s inflation-fighting message without signalling imminent action,” he wrote. “The speech arrives against a difficult policy backdrop. Inflation remains above target for a sixth consecutive year, while Fed officials have begun debating whether tighter policy may still be required.” Asian equity markets were broadly higher in early trade, with tech firms struggling to extend the Aug 27 rally that came on the back of Nvidia’s profit blowout and bumper forecast, which soothed worries over the AI boom. Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sydney, Singapore, Jakarta, Taipei and Mumbai all rose, though Seoul retreated along with Shanghai, Wellington, Bangkok and Manila. London, Paris and Frankfurt gained too. Wall Street had provided a positive lead, with all three main indexes rising, though the gains were based entirely on the technology sector, which was the only one of 11 to advance. Oil prices edged down but remain in danger of spiking further as investors await a breakthrough in efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tanker and cargo traffic. US officials have vowed further economic pressure to make Iran open the waterway – through which about a fifth of world oil passes – after six months of war , but attempts at a diplomatic solution remain elusive. events.title: Trump administration illegally retaliated against Anthropic, judge rules
events.summary: A judge has ruled the US Department of Defense acted unlawfully when it designated artificial intelligence (AI) startup Anthropic a supply chain risk, calling the move "illegal and baseless". The company argued in the lawsuit that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority with the new designation. It followed Anthropic's refusal to allow the military to use its AI models for tasks including surveillance or autonomous weapons. US District Judge Rita Lin said in the ruling that citing national security was "not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics". Anthropic welcomed the ruling. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon and the White House for comment. Anthropic was focused on "working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology", a spokesperson told the BBC. Judge Lin said in the court filing that the Defense Department had acted unlawfully to order firms that do business with the US military to boycott Anthropic. The Pentagon designated Anthropic as a supply-chain risk in February - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US. It marked the first time an American company had been publicly designated as such. Anthropic's lawsuit said the government's actions were both "unprecedented and unlawful". The Claude maker said its models were not reliable enough to be safely used in weapons systems for the military. It added that it opposed its use for domestic surveillance as a violation of rights. The Pentagon said at the time that private companies should not be able to constrain military action. The White House had previously said Anthropic was "a radical left, woke company attempting to control military activity" and argued the military was beholden to the US Constitution, "not any woke AI company's terms of service". The Pentagon also argued that Anthropic's refusal to accept new contract terms raised concerns over what the company could do with its technology. Anthropic said in its lawsuit that its business had been impacted by the government's actions and its right to freedom of speech had been violated. Judge Lin said during an earlier round in the lawsuit that the government was trying to "cripple" the company and "chill public debate" over military use of AI. "This appears to be classic First Amendment retaliation," the judge added. events.title: They were retrenched. Now they are among ground-up groups helping others find their footing
events.summary: (From left) Former Providore employee Fabian Soh and his former colleague Wong Yoon Loong, and Makan Minum Workers founder Kyle Ahmad. ST PHOTOS: CHONG JUN LIANG, KEVIN LIM Kyle Ahmad founded Makan Minum Workers (MMW) to support retrenched F&B workers by educating them about their rights and offering emotional and financial help. Local ground-up groups like Workers Make Possible and Migrant Workers Singapore also helped amplify MMW’s fundraising campaign on its platform to raise funds for about 80 former Twelve Cupcakes employees who needed the money for food and rental payments. These groups urge systemic changes, such as a statutory fund and legal accountability for employers, to better protect workers in sudden company closures. SINGAPORE – Kyle Ahmad worked as a bartender until his company suddenly wound up in 2023. “Our livelihoods were cut just like that,” the 38-year-old Singaporean told The Straits Times. Confused, he sought help from the Tripartite Alliance for Dispute Management (TADM). Months later, Kyle eventually received about half of the overtime pay he was owed. “It was definitely a stressful time,” he said, referring to the process of finding the right party for help and getting all the documents and evidence needed in order. The painful season inspired Kyle to set up Makan Minum Workers (MMW) in 2023 to help educate other food and beverage employees about their rights as well as advocate for these workers. “Makan” and “minum” are the Malay words for “eat” and “drink” respectively. MMW does not have an office. Any F&B worker, regardless of citizenship, can join for free. Today, it has more than 20 members. They gather for meals and outings from time to time, listen to one another’s experiences and proactively offer advice to other retrenched workers seeking guidance on their next steps. Makan Minum Workers founder Kyle Ahmad (left) met Suraendher Kumarr, a community worker at Workers Make Possible and now an active member of MMW, through a labour event in 2024. The friends subsequently collaborated on campaigns. An MMW member who wanted to be known only as Nee stepped up to help when she learnt that some Twelve Cupcakes employees had resorted to borrowing money from licensed moneylenders and loan sharks. She directed the affected workers to Blessed Grace Social Services, a non-profit organisation that offers recovery paths and debt solutions. Its case workers helped them negotiate a more structured and realistic repayment plan with their creditors. Confectionery chain Twelve Cupcakes suddenly shuttered in October 2025 , leaving about 80 workers in the lurch. After waiting for five months, these workers were told they would receive half of their owed salaries as the financially distressed company had insufficient funds for distribution. Nee herself was retrenched by cafe chain Providore five months ago, and knew the stress of losing one’s income suddenly. She had previously volunteered with Blessed Grace Social Services and was relatively familiar with some debt issues. Nee, who is in her mid-30s, said she herself received MMW’s support when she had a hard time coping with Providore’s sudden closure. “They gave me cash, and stood by my side whenever I needed help,” she said. In documents seen by ST, Nee and her former Providore colleague Fabian Soh are shown as still owed eight days of salary for March 2026. They were also not paid in lieu of notice or compensated for unutilised annual leave. Soh, 56, also joined MMW days after Providore suddenly wound up. “When I got retrenched, MMW helped me with my bills and expenses for my kids,” said the single father of two children, aged eight and 12. “But we don’t want to take advantage of them and keep asking for help.” Under MMW, Soh has so far also helped two former colleagues find new jobs through his network. Former Providore employee Fabian Soh (left) helped his former colleague Wong Yoon Loong (right) find a new job. Both are members of Makan Minum Workers. MMW works with other groups like Workers Make Possible and Migrant Workers Singapore to amplify workers’ voices through their platforms. Workers Make Possible, a group set up to help workers campaign for their rights, launched a crowdfunding campaign in 2021 to cover legal fees and provide financial aid for 10 Malaysian and three Singaporean bus drivers who sued their employer over alleged unfair workplace practices. Today, it has more than 100 volunteers. Suraendher Kumarr, a community worker with the group, said: “We fund-raise for things like the Labour Day rally or for workers in crisis.” He works freelance, in fields such as writing, research and project work, and food delivery. Suraendher Kumarr, 32, joined ground-up organisation Workers Make Possible in 2022 and is an active member of Makan Minum Workers. Not all workers know where and how they can find support, and the ground-up groups act as a friendlier bridge for workers to navigate the system here to seek help.

events.title: Bowen says 'no carve-outs' after Queensland claims data centre win
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Energy Minister says 'no carve-outs' after Queensland claims data centre win Chris Bowen has slapped down Queensland and the Northern Territory, insisting they have not been given a carve-out from new data centre rules. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Energy Minister Chris Bowen has rejected claims Queensland and the Northern Territory secured a carve-out from new rules requiring data centres to use 100 per cent renewables. States will be able to seek approval to use alternatives like coal or gas, but Mr Bowen says the Commonwealth will have the final say and the threshold will be "very high". The federal government will release draft national data centre standards before seeking to pass the legislation early next year. Queensland and the Northern Territory will not have control over how data centres are powered, the federal government insists, declaring there will be "no exceptions and no carve-outs" under its renewables plan. Energy and Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen told the ABC the national standards governing the development of data centres in Australia would still require them to bring their own "100 per cent" renewable energy plus firming through battery storage or gas. Mr Bowen has rejected claims this element of the Commonwealth's plan was watered down after a meeting of national cabinet on Wednesday where Queensland Premier David Crisafulli claimed a "win" that would allow his state to decide how data centres were powered. "So, as we said we would, we are legislating nationally consistent standards across the board with no exceptions and no carve-outs," Mr Bowen said. How Australia wants to be more than a data centre host Australia’s appeal as a destination for data centres has given it bargaining power in the AI boom. "The only change is that where a state owned government electricity company asserts that they can do it cheaper than renewables, they can apply to the Commonwealth to do that." In response, the Queensland government has now argued Mr Bowen's "rhetoric" was not contributing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's "goal" of proving a "positive path forward" on data centres. Premiers and chief ministers signed off on new data centre standards requiring data centre operators to invest in new renewable energy to offset their power usage, but also gave flexibility for state-owned electricity assets. This was widely interpreted as a capitulation to Queensland and the Northern Territory, which had both insisted they would not be dictated to by Canberra. Mr Bowen said it would be up to the Commonwealth to "decide" whether to let states use coal or gas as a main power source, and they would have to prove it was "cheaper and better for the grid than renewables would be". "[That] is a very high bar and very difficult to do, but some states may choose to do that," he said. Mr Bowen said the Australian Energy Regulator (AER), on behalf of the Commonwealth, would consider states' applications and "make a decision". "But we will be legislating those standards, which will apply equally in Queensland and the Northern Territory as everywhere else," he said. "I think it would be very, very difficult indeed for a state energy company to establish to the Commonwealth's satisfaction that a coal arrangement will be cheaper than renewables." David Crisafulli had claimed a "win" that would allow his state to decide how data centres were powered. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) In a statement on Friday, Queensland Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki said the purpose of the national data centre standards was to provide a "positive path forward and certainty for Australians, government and industry". "Chris Bowen's rhetoric is not contributing to that goal," he said. "The Queensland government will remain focused on the decisions made by national cabinet — acknowledging Queensland's unique position in owning generation and distribution assets and the energy mix that comes with that." Mr Janetzki said his government was "grateful for the maturity and pragmatism" shown by Mr Albanese. Following Wednesday's national cabinet meeting, Mr Crisafulli had told the ABC his state had been given a carve-out from the renewables policy. "It's a big win, not just for our economy, it's a big win for people's power bills as well," he said. "Because we own our assets, our distribution and our generation, we are able to control a different mixture of energy right across the board. "That new energy opportunity can be the abundance of gas we have, the surplus coal-fired power generation we have in the system, it can be renewable energy opportunities.

events.title: Embattled travel giant repaying tens of millions to overcharged clients
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Corporate Travel Management under pressure again after failing to pass on tens of millions of dollars in margins to clients Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Corporate Travel Management is refunding clients after failing to pass on travel supplier margins and rebates. ( Supplied: Corporate Travel Management ) Corporate Travel Management is in the process of refunding customers after pocketing tens of millions of dollars in margins and rebates that should have been passed onto clients. It's the latest headache for Corporate Travel, after the ABC earlier this month revealed a massive overcharging scandal relating to refugee accommodation in the UK. New chief executive Ana Pedersen says almost 80 per cent of the refunds have been agreed to or are near finalisation. An Australian travel giant arranging trips for governments and big business is in hot water after pocketing tens of millions of dollars in margins on air tickets and rebates from suppliers. Corporate Travel Management is now refunding the amounts to customers because contracts obliged the company to hand on some of this money to clients. For other customers, the problem is that contracts did not spell out what to do with the margins and so the cash is being handed back. The method of overcharging was revealed in an announcement from Brisbane-based Corporate Travel to the share market and brings the total of remediation to almost $246 million. Corporate Travel Management provides travel services to big businesses and governments. ( Supplied ) It is the latest installation of an imbroglio involving the sector repaying clients, with the ABC earlier revealing a secret government audit that warned of methods of overbilling. This latest overcharging at Corporate Travel is also separate to a massive overcharging scandal that had engulfed the company's dealings with the UK government for a refugee accommodation program. As the ABC revealed earlier this month, Corporate Travel's problems in the refugee contract included it invoicing the UK government more rooms than a hotel actually had, double-billing on some hotels, or charging for exclusive use of hotels when no exclusivity existed. Corporate Travel's new chief executive, Ana Pedersen, said almost 80 per cent of refunds had been agreed to or were near finalisation. "We recognise this has been a challenging period for investors, clients, partners and our people, and we are grateful for their ongoing support and confidence," she said. The company operated globally and clients have ranged from councils to big business, even the Australian and Queensland governments. The Queensland government said it was not one of the customers awaiting a refund. The Australian government said a review had not turned up evidence of systemic overcharging or retention of customer funds and the $13 million "relates to rebates payable to the New Zealand government". The New Zealand government declined to comment on specifics but said Corporate Travel had been cooperating about potential non-payment issues. New Corporate Travel Management CEO Ana Pedersen says it is a "challenging time" for the company and its clients. ( Supplied ) The latest overbilling included almost $29 million charged on European air fares, where Corporate Travel was buying some airline tickets and then selling them to clients with an additional margin. The company's accounts list "contractual ambiguity" here — management believed how customers were billed matched long-standing practices but now noted there was "uncertainty" about the company's contractual entitlement to keeping such margins. Another $13 million is from Australia and New Zealand, and associated with Corporate Travel keeping rebates from suppliers. Suppliers to travel management companies can be hotels, airlines or rental car firms, and they can provide commissions for bulk bookings. Corporate Travel has pocketed rebates from suppliers including hotels, airlines and rental car firms. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica ) The problem for Corporate Travel is some contracts required it to pass on rebates, and this was not done. Corporate Travel's accounts insisted that errors here were not from incorrectly billing customers. events.title: Regional powers seek off-ramp from Iran war, and other Middle East developments
events.summary: Qatar and other regional powers are seeking an off-ramp from the U.S. war Qatar and other regional powers sought an off-ramp from the war with Iran on Thursday as another tanker attack was reported in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Iranian government dismissed the Trump administration's latest sanctions. Elsewhere in the Middle East, Israel continued its attacks on Gaza and Lebanon even as the country's strikes on Gaza drew a sharp rebuke from the top diplomat overseeing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire in the territory. Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here . Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani was in Tehran on Thursday as part of Qatar's efforts to resolve the conflict between the United States and Iran. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said in a post on X that Al Thani's meeting with Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi included talks on “the efforts being made to reduce escalation,” as well as a proposed plan between Iran and Oman to allow ships safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and clear the vital commercial waterway of dangerous mines. Al Thani’s office said the prime minister emphasized the “necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighboring countries and the freedom of navigation” through the strait. He also met Thursday with Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian and its parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf. Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, underscored the longstanding ties between the two nations, noting that Iran supported Qatar during difficult times. Al Thani said Qatar has never hesitated to cooperate with Iran. U.S. President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that he has “no time schedule” to wrap up the conflict that will reach the six-month mark on Friday. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said Thursday that it had received a report of an oil tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz. The monitoring agency, run by the British military, said that local authorities reported that the vessel was hit by an unknown projectile on Tuesday in the waters between Oman and Iran, causing it to catch fire. The crew was reported to be safe and there have been no reports of environmental damage, the UKMTO said. Oil continues to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, albeit well below prewar levels, shipping analysts say. Ship traffic through the vital waterway increased last week compared with the prior week, with the number of oil and gas carriers up 50%, according to Lloyd’s List Intelligence. The U.S. government has claimed that up to 9 million barrels a day are flowing through the strait “over short time periods,” but commodities analysts at ING bank cautioned that the figure “seems aggressive.” Other ship-tracking estimates suggest it’s closer to 2 to 6 million barrels per day, ING said. Before the war, some 15 million barrels per day passed through the strait. Navy Admiral Bradley Cooper, the top U.S. military commander for the Middle East, said Thursday night that international shipping lanes through the Strait of Hormuz have been cleared of mines. “Today, international shipping lanes are open and momentum is building,” he said in a video posted on social media. Gulf states have not commented on the statement by U.S. Central Command, and it was not possible to independently verify the claim. Even without mines, however, ships still face threats from drones, missiles and boats as they pass through the narrow waterway. Esmail Baghaei, Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, wrote late Wednesday in a social media post that the U.S. had made a coalition with Bahrain, calling it a country with “virtually no meaningful economic exchange with Iran.” In another social media post on Wednesday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf thanked China for rejecting the U.S. “economic D-Day” policies against Iran. Dolly Parton’s sister reveals the singer’s touching final act of generosity 'It stood like a serpent': American who survived deadly Nepal flood tells her story 'She was suffering': Hayden Panettiere's mom details relationship during final months Earlier this week, Tehran had warned that it would respond harshly to expanded U.S. sanctions , including measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington. Days after the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced its dissolution, Syria’s interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa appointed the former SDF leader to a position as one of his advisers. SDF commander Mazloum Abdi on Tuesday announced that the SDF had completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force. The Kurdish-led force, which once controlled the country’s northeast, lost most of its territory to a government offensive in January and then signed the deal to merge with the army.

events.title: Advent, Stripe abandon $63.5b pursuit of fintech pioneer PayPal
events.summary: PayPal has struggled with modernising its payment technologies as rivals have seized market share. A consortium of Advent and Stripe has abandoned its pursuit of acquiring PayPal, ending a potential $63.5 billion deal. PayPal, an early digital payments pioneer, has struggled to modernise as competitors like Apple and Alphabet gained market share. PayPal's new CEO Enrique Lores aims to set clear financial goals and revenue targets to improve investor confidence amid past leadership changes. A consortium of buyout firm Advent and payment processor Stripe has decided to abandon its pursuit of fintech pioneer PayPal Holdings , a potential deal that would have ranked as one of the biggest ever leveraged buyouts, according to people familiar with the matter. The group is no longer pursuing a deal for PayPal , the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private. It had previously offered more than US$50 billion (S$63.5 billion) for the company, people with knowledge of the matter have said. Founded in the late 1990s, PayPal was an early mover in digital payments. It has since struggled with modernising its payment technologies as rivals such as Apple and Alphabet have seized market share. Bloomberg News first revealed in February that Stripe was considering an acquisition of parts or all of PayPal, after a stock slump wiped out a chunk of its value. The takeover interest, coupled with second-quarter earnings that topped analyst estimates, has helped it recover. PayPal shares have jumped more than 40 per cent this quarter, giving the company a market value of about US$52.6 billion. San Jose, California-based PayPal ousted former chief executive Alex Chriss earlier in 2026 and replaced him with Enrique Lores, who took over the role in March. Lores said he will set specific financial goals for PayPal, change how the payments company reports earnings and assign each line of business a specific revenue target to give investors a better sense of their potential. The Wall Street Journal reported in August that PayPal had found Advent and Stripe’s initial bid insufficient and the two sides were negotiating a potential higher price. Advent and Stripe could always opt to come back at a later date if the situation changes. Representatives for Advent, PayPal and Stripe declined to comment. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Judge blocks Pentagon's Anthropic blacklist
events.summary: A federal judge on Thursday struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk , ruling that the government's actions violated Anthropic's constitutional rights. Why it matters: The ruling marks a major legal victory for Anthropic in its months-long fight with the Trump administration over how the military can use its AI models. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Rita Lin ruled that the Pentagon's designation of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk was unlawful. "The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics," Lin wrote in her 59-page decision. "Though the Department of War is undisputedly free to select the AI vendor of its choice, the evidence demonstrates that the broad measures imposed on Anthropic were illegal and baseless." Lin noted that the Pentagon continued pursuing work with Anthropic even after the designation: "None of that is consistent with a genuine fear that Anthropic is a saboteur who would poison its software to harm national security." What they're saying: "We welcome the court's ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful," an Anthropic spokesperson said in a statement. "We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology." Catch up quick: The dispute kicked off earlier this year after Anthropic and the Pentagon clashed over the military's use of the company's AI models. The Defense Department sought to use Claude for "all lawful purposes," even in the most sensitive military and intelligence applications. Anthropic insisted that two areas remain off-limits: mass surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous weapons. The standoff escalated, with the Pentagon designating Anthropic a national security and supply-chain risk, leading the AI company to sue. What's next: The government is expected to appeal the ruling. Anthropic is also fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit.

events.title: Chinese battery giant CATL spreads investments in search of new growth drivers
events.summary: World’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for EVs and energy storage systems has committed over 17 billion yuan to non-battery deals Since June last year, at least seven CATL-led equity deals involving a total of over 17 billion yuan (US$2.5 billion) have been announced in non-battery industries. The sectors involved span humanoid robots, state-owned hydropower stations, artificial intelligence data centres (AIDCs) and large-language-model developer DeepSeek. The equity investments by Fujian-based CATL seemed primarily strategic, similar to its earlier playbook of forming joint ventures with carmakers and investing in EV start-ups, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings. “As the incumbent leader, sustaining market share and margins requires identifying new high-growth frontiers early and capturing first-mover advantages,” she said. “AIDC’s high-growth, high-barrier characteristics position it as a potential ‘third growth curve’ alongside EVs and energy storage systems.” CATL is the world’s largest producer of lithium-ion batteries for EVs and energy storage systems. But it is facing weakening demand for electric cars in China – the world’s largest automotive market – and intensifying competition with domestic rivals for energy storage orders in overseas markets. In May, Nasdaq-listed VNET Group, a Chinese third-party provider of neutral data centres, said two CATL-affiliates would acquire up to 38.1 per cent of its shares for US$942 million, becoming its largest shareholder. This month, Shenzhen-listed Hangzhou Zhonhen Electric, which supplies power supply systems for data centres and vehicle charging, said that it planned to sell a 49 per cent stake in the business to CATL for 4.09 billion yuan.

events.title: Major private credit fund suspends investor redemptions
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Private credit firm CVS Lane joins list of firms limiting investor pullouts Topic: Business, Economics and Finance Private credit firm CVS Lane says it had significant loans to collapsed property developer Bathla. ( Supplied: Bathla website ) Stress in Australia's private credit sector is intensifying. A private lender with significant loans to collapsed developer Bathla called CVS Lane is the latest private credit firm to limit "investor redemptions". The ABC has confirmed that the investment manager told investors on Thursday that its CVS Lane First Mortgage Fund and CVS Lane Property Finance Fund had exposure to Bathla across nine different loans. Investor redemptions are when investors in private credit firms seek to get some or all of their money returned in the face of concerns about the safety of their investment because of potentially overly risky lending. Major Sydney residential developer Bathla Group announced earlier this week that it was going into administration after months of mounting financial pressure, owning more than $3.5 billion. Major NSW developer enters administration Bathla Group says tax changes, softening sales and construction costs have led to its plight. Administrators from Teneo were appointed to its main corporate entity, Universal Property Group, as well as Raj & Jai Construction, a company linked to the Bathla Group, documents lodged with ASIC show. CVS Lane is reported to have told investors it had "determined to temporarily suspend the processing of application and redemption requests across the funds". "The funds' redemption provisions are designed to balance investor liquidity with the interests of all investors in the funds," it told clients. Temporary suspension 'in best interests' CVS Lane has $2.1 billion under management. "The trustee considers a temporary suspension to be in the best interests of investors as a whole, with relevant factors including the current uncertainty surrounding the Bathla administration and the need to ensure any decisions … are made on the basis of the best available information," CVS Lane is reported to have told investors. There are about 40 private credit funds invested in Bathla, with exposures ranging from $1.5 million to $340 million. CVS Lane told investors it would update them next week and reassess its position by the end of October. Among the other private credit firms exposed to Bathla, the ABC has contacted Balmain, Centuria Bass, Credit Connect, CVS Lane, Keyview, La Trobe, Ray White Capital and Trilogy for comment. The ABC understands private credit firm Keyview's loans are at the stage of being repaid through the settlement of completed assets rather than having any exposure to Bathla's ongoing viability. The Sydney-based firm, according to its website, oversees more than $800 million across its funds. The ABC understand Keyview has no redemption restrictions in place across any of its funds and has no current plans to limit investor liquidity. La Trobe Financial's total exposure to the Bathla Group is approximately $38.1 million. "It comprises four residential loans and one development loan," the firm said in a statement. The development project is approximately 95 per cent complete. The private credit firm added: "We hold the full costs to complete it, and presales cover 89 per cent of the current loan balance. "We expect to recover the loan in full." Trilogy Funds said that, as of yesterday, its exposure to Bathla Group was $29.79 million, relating to two of 131 current loans. "Trilogy Monthly Income Trust continues to operate in the normal course and there are currently no plans to limit investor redemptions," the private lender said in answer to the ABC News questions about the potential for investor redemptions. "Redemption procedures remain unchanged and investors continue to have access to their funds in accordance with normal processes." Concerns more credit provide will limit redemptions Credit funds not exposed to Bathla have told the ABC they are concerned more private credit providers will limit redemptions to avoid investors pulling money out now in fear of not being able to later on. Earlier this week MA Financial announced a temporary redemption limit of up to 1 per cent of its funds under management per month. Bathla Group seeks $20m to keep building Bathla Group's collapse leaves buyers and builders waiting for answers. MA Financial's joint chief executive Chris Wyke told Nine newspapers the action was a "proactive measure in response to the potential for increased redemption activity".

events.title: Scoop: National Democrats and Republicans squeeze local TV stations in ad rate war
events.summary: National Democrats and Republicans are pressuring local TV stations to respond in opposite ways to a new federal court ruling on political ad rates, Axios has learned. Why it matters: How they respond will have a major impact on the fight for control of Congress by deciding which party's ad money goes further in the final stretch of the 2026 midterms . The 4th Circuit Court of Appeals this week overturned an FCC rule extending discounted ad rates for individual congressional campaigns to political parties and super PACs. In other words: The court ruled that outside groups still have to fork over multiple times what the actual candidates pay to run political ads. Democrats tend to do their strongest fundraising at the candidate level while Republicans generally dominate national party and super PAC spending, meaning the decision was a win for Democrats. Driving the news: A pair of Democratic media buyers warned TV stations in a letter first obtained by Axios that they could face legal consequences if they offer discounted rates to outside groups. Doing so "may raise campaign finance concerns," wrote Miles King of Amplify Media and Bradley Perseke of GMMB, because it "risks making an unlawful, unreported corporate in-kind contribution." "Please confirm at your earliest convenience the rates your station intends to offer political party committees and joint fundraising committees for the remainder of the election cycle," they continued. Amplify Media and GMMB work with a slew of Democratic campaigns and groups including the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee — the House and Senate Democratic campaign arms. Between the lines: Democrats are looking at the federal court ruling as a much-needed win after the Supreme Court ruling last month overturned limits on what political parties could spend in coordination with campaigns. That decision, like the FCC ad rate rule, benefited Republicans' top-heavy fundraising structure in which the national party plays an outsized role. Julie Merz and Devan Barber, the executive directors of the DCCC and DSCC, respectively, said in a statement their groups "dealt Republicans a major blow in their latest attempt to rig the rules in their favor." They added, "Democratic candidates' strong grassroots fundraising amplifying the voice of everyday Americans remains a fundamental advantage in the midterms, and our stronger candidates and better campaigns will secure us House and Senate majorities in November." The other side: Ryan Dollar and Blake Murphy, the top lawyers for the National Republican Congressional Committee and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, wrote to TV stations that the Democratic letter "should be disregarded." In a letter first obtained by Axios, the two attorneys argued that neither the 4th Circuit Ruling nor Federal Election Commission guidance prohibit stations from offering the discounted rate to outside groups voluntarily. "Broadcasters have long exercised discretion regarding advertising rates in circumstances where an advertiser was not necessarily entitled to a particular statutory benefit," they wrote. What to watch: Dollar and Murphy made their own legal threats, arguing that under Democrats' interpretation of the ruling TV stations have "likely committed years of campaign finance violations" whenever they offered discounted rate to outside groups. "Should your station choose to ... adopt Democrats' campaign finance logic, we intend to file FEC complaints against your station for all advertising you have previously offered," they wrote. Republicans also intend to appeal the 4th Circuit ruling to the Supreme Court, the attorneys said, adding that they "intend to pursue all available remedies to recoup any financial losses should the [FCC] rule be restored."

events.title: Military veterans told they owe thousands of pounds over clerical error
events.summary: Royal Navy veteran Andrew Thorburn has been told he owes more than £26,000 Hundreds of former members of the military have had their pensions slashed after receiving letters telling them to repay thousands of pounds because of a clerical error. The Ministry of Defence (MoD) confirmed to the BBC that more than 1000 retired service personnel are being pursued for debts. The majority, 335 veterans, were overpaid a total of £5.1m as a result of incorrect National Insurance calculations. The Forces Pension Society said it is aware of a small number of veterans whose debts were wiped after raising a formal complaint. Ray Lawton, 70, was told in July he owed £8,000 following six years of overpayments. Days later, his monthly military pension was cut from £550 to £365. Royal Artillery veteran Ray Lawton has been ordered to repay £8,000 "I haven't got £8,000 to pay out," said Lawton, who served 16 years in the Royal Artillery. "I've got a little bit put aside but nowhere near that much." The Portsmouth-based veteran told the BBC: "I've trusted the army all my life even when I left and I trusted my pension would be right. Then this letter comes and it's just blown it all out." Lawton's letter was sent from a company called Equiniti, which administers the pension scheme on behalf of the MoD. It said an error in its system meant he had been overpaid for years. Lawton is one of many veterans from across the UK who contacted BBC Your Voice after receiving letters out of the blue seeking money they didn't know they owed. The Forces Pension Society, a not-for-profit which supports military retirees, said it is aware of many overpayment cases running into the tens of thousands of pounds. A small number of veterans have been told they owe six-figure sums. The MoD confirmed errors relating to National Insurance adjustments, Pension Sharing Orders (PSO), Early Departure Payments (EDP) and State Pension Age (SPA). It says it is investigating issues on a case-by-case basis. It added that of the 335 veterans affected by National Insurance errors, a third have paid off their debt in full and 52 have an agreed repayment plan in place. So far, of the £5.1m, £304,000 has been paid back. Veterans said they want more clarity about the debt and how it has been calculated. Some have called for it to be wiped. The government said it has a responsibility to recover the funds. An MoD spokesperson told the BBC that it recognises that errors to pension payments "may cause uncertainty", adding that it is contacting veterans and "providing support for anyone who requires it". "Where payments have been made in genuine error, we have a responsibility to recover taxpayer funds and will always seek to do so in a sensitive and proportionate way," the spokesperson added. However, former Conservative defence secretary Penny Mordaunt, said: "While public bodies have a duty to recoup such costs if it makes financial sense to do so, no such assessment has been made in these cases. "There is a compelling case in many instances for the debt to be wiped". Andrew Thorburn says the financial shock has been "absolutely devastating" Lawton does not want the taxpayer to pick up the tab, he is happy to have his pension reduced to the level it should have been but thinks the private company should refund the bill for what he sees as their mistake. "I think they should take responsibility for it because it's not my fault." He served 36 years in the Royal Navy and has been told he owes £26,438. As a result, his pension has been cut by around £650 per month. "I think it's despicable that they are now saying 'yes, we've made this mistake however you're going to pay for it'. How can I forgive the government for that?" He said: "The financial shock is absolutely devastating and it's still ongoing." Barrie Goodwin said the impact of repaying £32,000 would be very difficult RAF veteran Barrie Goodwin contacted Equiniti six years ago after receiving a higher payment than he was expecting. He was told the change was because he had reached state pension age. He's since been notified he was overpaid £32,188 and must hand it back. "I checked, was told it was all correct and now have to repay it," he said. "I'm already cutting back on luxuries. I was helping one of my grandchildren through nursery - that's had to change. "If the debt isn't waived, I will really struggle." Equiniti told the BBC it could not discuss individual cases but recognised the concern caused to pensioners. A spokesperson said it was not responsible for the decision to recoup taxpayers' money but "administration of a scheme of this scale involves multiple organisations, systems and processes over many years". Technology company Sopra Steria has been in charge of the veterans' pension scheme since 2023, and had subcontracted the administration to Equiniti.

events.title: Tiger, Futu post strong overseas gains after Beijing clampdown stalls mainland growth
events.summary: Brokerages shift to Southeast Asia, US and Europe amid Beijing’s stepped-up drive to root out illegal cross-border securities activity Tiger Brokers and Futu Holdings, two of the region’s largest online brokerages, posted robust second-quarter growth as they expanded overseas to absorb Beijing’s toughest crackdown yet on illegal cross-border stock trading. UP Fintech Holding, parent of Tiger Brokers, reported on Wednesday that revenue rose 31.4 per cent year on year to a record US$182.3 million. Net income attributable to shareholders, however, slipped to US$39.4 million from US$41.4 million a year earlier. “To streamline users’ compliance procedures and reduce tax declaration complexities, we rolled out a dedicated tax reporting tool under our Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand regulatory licences,” Wu said in an exchange filing, adding that Tiger also rolled out fractional share trading for Singapore-listed stocks and index options trading in Hong Kong. Hong Kong client assets grew almost 30 per cent quarter on quarter after Tiger stepped up offline client-acquisition campaigns, while assets in the US jumped nearly 50 per cent and those in Australia and New Zealand rose more than 30 per cent. Futu, which reported last week, posted revenue of HK$7.2 billion (US$918 million), up 35.6 per cent, and net income attributable to the shareholders of HK$3.64 billion, up 41.6 per cent. Funded accounts expanded 33.6 per cent to 3.84 million, led for a third straight quarter by Malaysia, with Hong Kong and Singapore also among the top contributors.

events.title: Iran braces for unrest amid economic crisis
events.summary: The US campaign to inflict economic pain on Iran is squeezing the Iranian people, but is unlikely to move their leaders to end the war, analysts argued. The threat of sanctions triggered panic buying for food and fuel this week, The Wall Street Journal reported, sparking small labor demonstrations across Iran. Inflation hit 66% in July and food prices soared 128% year on year, raising concerns among Iranian leaders that economic grievances could once again fuel mass protests that have erupted nationwide in recent years. Washington hopes to leverage such public discontent into forcing Tehran to cut a peace deal, Reuters wrote, but “the leadership has historically answered domestic unrest with repression , and external pressure with threats of retaliation abroad.” — Tasneem Nashrulla

events.title: Hackers use SpaceX's Cursor AI agent in cyber break-ins
events.summary: Russian-speaking hackers used SpaceX’s Cursor AI agent to breach a Belgian chemical company and six other firms in recent months, in the latest instance of cybercriminals circumventing AI firms’ safety guardrails. The hackers recruited the agent for hundreds of attacks by telling it the exercises were part of a simulation, Reuters reported, making their work up to 50% faster. The agent, powered by an Anthropic model, at one point recommended the hackers use a common malware tool to break into a German manufacturer. The report comes as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and 100 other companies signed an open letter Thursday warning of a “ limited window to strengthen cyber defenses ” as AI-enabled cyber attacks are set to proliferate in the coming months. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Scoop: Democrats plan bill to counter Trump order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America"
events.summary: House Democrats are planning legislation to counteract the executive order President Trump signed Thursday redesignating Lake Ontario as "Lake America," Axios has learned. Why it matters: Democrats are scrambling to contain the fallout from an escalating economic conflict between the Trump administration and the Canadian government. The collapse of trade talks between the two countries last week triggered 50% tariffs on a slew of Canadian goods, to which Canada has vowed to respond in kind. Driving the news: Rep. Tim Kennedy (D-N.Y.), who co-chairs the bipartisan Northern Border Caucus, told Axios in a text message that he is "working on a bill" to respond to Trump's order. Kennedy is one of numerous Democrats who have denounced the renaming, saying in a statement it is evidence that Trump is a "petty, vindictive, failed president." White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers, in a statement to Axios responding to Kennedy, said: "Does the Congressman not love America?" Zoom in: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.), the chair of House Democrats' messaging arm, told Politico she also plans to introduce a bill reversing the executive order. Dingell, a vocal critic of Trump's trade war with Canada, said of the "Lake America" order in a radio interview on Thursday: "I think it's absolutely insane, and I deeply resent it." Catch up quick: The executive order Trump signed directs the Interior Department to update the Geographic Names Information System within 30 days to reflect the name change. "In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation's economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America," the order said. Trump has previously ordered the federal government to refer to the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America," though it remains unclear if he has the power to rename a body of water shared by multiple countries. Canadian officials have said they will not honor the name change. Reality check: With Republicans in control of both chambers of Congress, Democrats will likely have trouble securing a chance to vote on their legislation. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional reporting.

events.title: Trump’s trade war hands Democrats a campaign-trail gift
events.summary: The News FARMINGTON HILLS, Mich. — President Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada is handing a political gift to Democrats in this pivotal battleground state. Democratic candidates across Michigan are unifying against Trump’s 50% tariffs on an array of Canadian goods, hitching Republicans to a trade battle against a trusted neighbor that polls show is unpopular. The alignment is a helpful way for Democrats to change the subject from US-Israel policy, a topic that has bitterly split them in this state in particular. Taking on Trump over Canada trade also helps Democrats sidestep their own past divisions on the issue. The party has long cleaved between pro-business factions and labor allies, and some Democrats — especially in Michigan — remain open to targeted tariffs, not to mention critical of free trade pacts. But at the moment, in a swing state that counts Canada as its top export destination, Democrats are focused on where they agree. “These tariffs are simply about [Trump’s] ego, and he wants us to have to pay for them. And Mike Rogers is going to do nothing but rubber-stamp it,” Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, told supporters Wednesday at a packed banquet hall in the Detroit suburbs. El-Sayed spent both of his appearances in southeast Michigan decrying Rogers, his Republican opponent, as tacitly supportive of Trump’s hefty new tariffs. The levies have so far hit Canadian steel and could affect autos by January. His opposition to Trump’s approach doesn’t extend to all tariffs, however. In an interview with Semafor after his campaign stops, El-Sayed likened past free trade agreements with Canada and Mexico, like NAFTA and USMCA, to “cancers on the American economy. I oppose them outright.” “But the response isn’t just tariffs willy-nilly because you got mad at the prime minister,” El-Sayed added. “The response is a thoughtful, direct tariff policy, akin to chemotherapy for cancer.” He suggested a targeted, “goal-oriented” use of tariffs to protect certain “high growth potential industries,” rolling them back when certain trade benchmarks were met. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment. Know More The new tariffs’ impact on the cross-border supply chain threatens an auto industry that’s essential to the Michigan economy. Michigan exported $21.2 billion in goods to Canada last year, according to the US trade representative’s office; it’s among the US states most reliant on Canadian trade. Industry representatives in the state are openly warning of electoral consequences for Republican candidates from Trump’s tariffs in multiple states that do significant business with Canada. “The White House’s strategy makes it a lot more difficult … because you have to kind of explain away what this White House’s strategy is,” said the Detroit Regional Chamber of Commerce’s Sandy Baruah, formerly a George W. Bush administration official. It’s not just El-Sayed making the most of the opportunity to hammer Trump’s trade tactics. Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson is linking Republican opponent John James to them at every turn, dubbing the Canada tariffs a “John James tax.” In a battleground manufacturing-heavy House district in the Detroit suburbs, Democratic nominee Christina Hines said that “Canada is not the problem.” Hines used her opposition to the tariffs to cast her Republican opponent Mike Bouchard as a loyalist who “falls in line” with Trump. “He’s a really nice young man, but he supports everything that this president does,” she said. “What we need is someone that’s actually going to stand up and fight for us.” Bouchard, in a statement, framed the tariffs as one chapter in negotiations. “For too long, adversarial nations like China have been taking advantage of Canada and America,” Bouchard said. “The President is a great negotiator and is defending American manufacturing. I am hopeful we can resolve this quickly, reach a deal beneficial to both countries, and have fair trade between us. They are an important trading partner and ally.” The View From Canada Across the border, Canadians are digging in for long-term pain at the hands of their onetime ally. Canada has responded with its own retaliatory tariffs and pledged an aid package for affected companies, with Prime Minister Mark Carney commanding public support for the economic pain that will result from pushing back. “We’ve had the sand kicked in our face for the last two years, and we reached a point, because Canadians are notorious for being civil and tolerant — that it’s a breaking point now,” Mike Bradley, the mayor of Sarnia, Ontario, told Semafor in an interview in his office just across the Blue Water Bridge from Port Huron, Mich. “If you think about it,” he added, “most of the economic consequences are going to be on both sides of the border.” Sarnia, a petrochemical center, was already feeling the sting of Trump’s past trade clashes with Canada before the most recent escalation. Bradley called Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario “not that funny” anymore, adding a note of pessimism about the future even after a new president takes office. The US-Canada bond is “like a relationship that goes sideways, and sometimes you can get it back on track, but it’s never usually the same as it was before,” he said. “And sometimes you get divorced.” The View From Republicans Michigan Republicans have largely kept their heads down amid the trade war. Many in the party are generally opposed to tariffs, though some have joined Bouchard in portraying the Canada levies as a negotiating tactic. Rogers and other Republicans have focused instead on Democrats’ associations with controversial left-wing streamer Hasan Piker. El-Sayed put distance between himself and Piker on Wednesday following intraparty condemnation of Piker’s comments on American Jews. Nicholas’s view Democrats everywhere, and especially in Michigan, rightly see Trump’s Canada tariffs as a useful unforced error this close to the election. But their agreement on trade isn’t guaranteed to hold should they take power in the Capitol, or reclaim the White House in 2028. Powerful allied groups like the UAW support other tariffs that are aimed at bringing manufacturing jobs back to the US, presaging tough choices ahead for the party. Former President Joe Biden kept many of Trump’s first-term tariffs in place , after all. Bradley, the Canadian mayor, also noticed the conundrum facing the American opposition. “The Democrats should be hitting home runs every day, but the split in the party — you don’t know which Democratic Party is going to be winning in November,” he said. He added a caveat on the new tariffs: “I haven’t seen one Republican of the courage to stand up, at any level elected, to say ‘We do not support this.’” Notable Some of the most profitable cars made by Detroit’s automakers could be hit by the tariffs, The Wall Street Journal reported . events.title: Taiwan approves $7 billion drone budget
events.summary: Taiwan’s legislature approved a plan to spend more than $7 billion on drones over the next six years, part of the island’s push to deter a potential attack from China. President Lai Ching-te’s administration views drones as critical to Taiwan’s “ porcupine strategy ” — asymmetric warfare using small, agile, and cheap defense systems to inflict pain on larger aggressors. Taiwan’s drone manufacturing has largely been scaled for export, but the new budget — although watered down — could boost domestic demand for drones and strengthen local supply chains, allowing the sector to mass produce drones even under bombardment. Taiwan’s vice president noted the island was inspired by how Ukraine had built up its drone capabilities from the “ battlefield of blood and tears. ” — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Russia-Ukraine war enters deadlier phase
events.summary: The Russia-Ukraine war has entered a more dangerous and deadly phase, analysts said, as the countries’ degraded aerial defenses contend with intensifying missile and drone barrages. Deaths have mounted in recent weeks as Ukraine runs dry of Patriot interceptors and Russia increasingly targets Kyiv’s civilian logistics, raising concerns that Moscow could force emigration by starving swathes of Ukraine of food and electricity . Kyiv, meanwhile, aims to sow economic discontent among Russians with strikes against oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses , but experts argued domestic upheaval is unlikely to change Moscow’s calculus. With the frontlines frozen and both sides mounting more long-range strikes, the war “will get steadily more destructive without being decisive ,” a military analyst told The Wall Street Journal. — Brendan Ruberry

events.title: Iran braces for economic unrest
events.summary: The US campaign to inflict economic pain on Iran is squeezing the Iranian people, but is unlikely to move their leaders to end the war, analysts argued . The threat of sanctions triggered panic buying for food and fuel this week, The Wall Street Journal reported, sparking small labor demonstrations across Iran. Inflation hit 66% in July and food prices soared 128% year on year, raising concerns among Iranian leaders that economic grievances could once again fuel mass protests that have erupted nationwide in recent years. Washington hopes to leverage such public discontent into forcing Tehran to cut a peace deal, Reuters wrote, but “the leadership has historically answered domestic unrest with repression , and external pressure with threats of retaliation abroad.” — Tasneem Nashrulla

events.title: Delivery company restarts services to regional Tasmania after resident complaints
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Team Global Express reinstates delivery services to regional Tasmania after resident complaints Topic: Postal and Delivery Services Team Global Express has reinstated the delivery services it cut to parts of regional Tasmania. ( Team Global Express ) Team Global Express has reversed its decision to stop delivering to parts of regional Tasmania. Residents had told the ABC they were forced to spend hours on the road to collect their deliveries from the depot, despite paying for a door-to-door service. The company's executive chair, Christine Holgate, visited Miena in central Tasmania to speak with an affected resident and tell him the deliveries would restart. A delivery company has reinstated services to regional Tasmania, after residents raised complaints with the ABC. In recent months, Team Global Express stopped delivering online orders to Miena, Liawenee, Waddamana, Levendale, Tunnack, Bradys Lake, Bronte Park, Derwent Bridge, Lake St Clair, Maydena and Colebrook. Despite paying for deliveries to be sent to their homes, residents received text messages saying they had seven days to pick up their packages from the company's depot at Hobart Airport . The company cited operational challenges for its drivers as the reason for the decision, including unsafe road conditions in winter. On Thursday, the executive chair of Team Global Express, Christine Holgate, flew to Tasmania to visit Miena resident Michael Walls, who had told the ABC he was not willing to make a four-hour round trip to collect his packages when he had paid for delivery. For Michael Walls, the round trip to pick up his packages from the Hobart depot would have taken four hours. ( ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough ) Mr Walls said the visit was a success. "Ms Holgate confirmed that Team Global Express has reversed their decision to stop delivering to large parts of central Tasmania," he told ABC Northern Tasmania. "Team Global Express will now resume [delivering] to all areas they previously cancelled. "Ms Holgate also said she would like to apologise to their customers for this decision and said it was their local Tasmanian management decision to cancel the service and that it was not known by their national office. Christine Holgate visited Miena on Thursday to speak with an affected resident. ( ABC News: Marcus Stimson ) A spokesperson for the company confirmed the reversal. "Christine is very grateful to Michael for raising the matter," they said. The Tasmanian government welcomed the decision, saying it was an example of what could be achieved when regional communities made their voices heard and businesses were prepared to listen. "This is a very welcome outcome for people living and doing business in rural and regional Tasmania," Consumer Affairs Minister Guy Barnett said. "Reliable freight and parcel delivery services are crucial in rural communities, where residents and small businesses may otherwise face hours of travel simply to collect an item they have paid to have delivered. "I thank Team Global Express executive chair Christine Holgate for taking the time to come to Tasmania, listening to the concerns raised on behalf of our regional communities and acting quickly to find a way forward.

events.title: The world wants to build data centres in Australia, but we want something in return
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Australia in a 'sliding doors' moment to determine who reaps rewards of AI boom Andrew Charlton says Australia has become a very attractive destination for data centres. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Australia's growing appeal as a destination for data centres has given it rare bargaining power as global tech giants race to build AI infrastructure. Local AI companies want the federal government to use that leverage to secure affordable computing power so Australian businesses can capitalise on the boom. The government says this is a "sliding doors" moment as it launches a new partnership to get major Australian companies buying more locally developed AI technology. Christopher Sampson had to take his Australian artificial intelligence (AI) startup Tiliter overseas before customers at home would take it seriously. For Michael Gately, scaling up his AI company from Australia has meant competing in a global scramble for expensive and increasingly sought-after computing power. Both chief executives have found ways around these business constraints. Still, their experiences highlight the challenges Australia faces as it tries to capture more of the economic gains from AI. Christopher Sampson (left) and his co-CEO Marcel Herz had to find customers abroad before Australian companies would buy their AI technology. ( Supplied ) Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton has declared Australia is at a "sliding doors" moment to ensure the country becomes a "creator" rather than a "renter" of AI. The nation's AI startups agree and want Australia to leverage its advantage as an attractive destination for data centres to negotiate guaranteed and affordable access to computing power. Australian companies are reliant on the small number of businesses that control the world's advanced computing capacity, generated by electricity-hungry data centres. ( Supplied ) How Australia can get a 'return' for hosting data centres Australian companies currently are heavily reliant on the small number of tech businesses that control the world's advanced computing capacity. That capacity is generated by large electricity-hungry data centres. Australia has become a very attractive place to host these centres. The federal government is in the process of developing national standards to govern the approval of data centre projects, which have increasingly attracted community backlash. Working with states and territories, the government will establish rules around their location and their use of electricity and water. Once built, data centres employ relatively few people directly, which means simply hosting them does not guarantee Australia a large share of the economic benefits they enable. The federal government has unveiled a new "Buy Australian AI Partnership" to help local AI companies win customers. ( ABC News: Supplied ) But Mr Charlton has argued Australia does have the bargaining power to dictate better terms. "If you want to build a data centre in Australia, you should be prepared to make some of that compute available to Australian businesses, researchers and startups," he said in a speech this month. Mr Charlton said this would ensure Australia got a greater "return" from the AI boom. Australian companies urged to buy local AI technology Computing power is not the only hurdle, however, with many Australian AI startups struggling to find domestic buyers to support their companies. Yesterday, the federal government unveiled a new "Buy Australian AI Partnership" backed by the nation's Big Four banks to help local AI companies win customers. Mr Charlton said the more than 1,500 Australian AI companies were already building "world-class" technology, but the challenge was getting in front of the organisations that could buy their product. "We are in a sliding doors moment for Australia's AI industry," he said. Behind the energy brawl everyone wants the data centre boom As is so often the case in Australia, the politics came down to a fight over energy. "As the importance of this technology grows, we need to ensure Australia is a creator and not just renter of AI." The difficulty convincing Australian businesses to buy local AI products is well known to the Tiliter co-chief executive Mr Sampson, whose company creates vision software widely used by retailers, including for self-checkouts. He said it took proving his technology in international markets to get "validity" back in Australia. "Fortunately, I had a German co-founder, which gave us access to that market," Mr Sampson told the ABC. "If I didn't, I'm not sure I would have taken that step.

events.title: Trump moves to rename Lake Ontario to "Lake America"
events.summary: President Trump signed an executive order renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America" on Thursday. Why it matters: The president is following through on his threat over the lake after U.S.-Canada trade negotiations collapsed. The collapse triggered 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, with Canada announcing matching tariffs set to take effect Sept. 8. Catch up quick: Trump has repeatedly posted on social media in recent days about renaming the lake , once writing that America doesn't "expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer." He's also posted images showing the lake renamed "Lake America." By the numbers: Roughly 47% of the lake that straddles the border with the Canadian province of Ontario lies within the U.S. What they're saying: "The United States is the greatest protector of the Great Lakes , including the body of water currently known as Lake Ontario," Trump wrote in the executive order. "The Lake will continue to play a pivotal role in shaping America's future and the global economy. In recognition of this flourishing economic resource and its critical importance to our Nation's economy and its people, I am directing that the Lake officially be renamed as Lake America." The other side: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted in a post on X that the lake's name is an anglicized version of an Indigenous word that predates the establishment of the Canadian province of Ontario, as he pushed back on Trump's order: Screenshot: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney/X How it works: The order directs Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and his department to update the Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) to reflect the renaming of the Lake within 30 days. It requires all federal government references to the lake refer to the body of water as "Lake America" moving forward. The big picture: It is unclear whether Trump has the authority to rename a body of water shared between two nations, as he did last year when he signed a similar order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the " Gulf of America ." The order can't compel Canada to call the shared body of water "Lake America," and Canadian officials have said they won't. More from Axios: Scoop: Dems plan bill to counter Trump's "Lake America" order "Lake America": Trump turns Canada feud toward Lake Ontario Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.
